item.title: 49ers considered favorites to win NFC West after Week 1
item.description: The Niners have made a big jump in the NFC West odds.
item.content:encoded:
Through one week, the NFC West is 3-1, with the lone loss being the Los Angeles Rams, who fell to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia.

While the spread was 3.5-points, not many had faith in the 49ers, myself included, after the Rams added a ton of star talent in the offseason, making them the odds-on favorites to win the Super Bowl.

With the Super Bowl-winning Seattle Seahawks still around with their nucleus of players, they were also considered above the 49ers for both the NFC West and the Super Bowl. But things have quickly shifted after Week 1, when the 49ers beat the Rams 27-7 and showed the potential of what their team can do when healthy.

According to ESPN, the 49ers have jumped from third to first in NFC West odds, climbing up to +160 odds to win the division. The Seahawks are shortly behind at +175, and the Rams, who were hovering around +100 to begin the season, are now third at +205 odds.

However, that hasn’t changed the big-picture outlook as much. ESPN still has the Rams as the odds-on favorites to win the Super Bowl at +650, while the 49ers are tied for the fifth-best odds with the Kansas City Chiefs at +1400. Ahead of them are the Baltimore Ravens (+900), Buffalo Bills (+950), and Seattle Seahawks (+1100).

It’s interesting that oddsmakers don’t see the Rams as the NFC West division winner, but they do still have them as the favorite to win the Super Bowl. The 49ers, however, do have better odds to win the NFC than the Seahawks.

Los Angeles is seen as the favorite to make the Super Bowl out of the NFC at +455, while the 49ers jump up to second with +550 odds. The Seahawks are shortly behind at +580, while the Philadelphia Eagles (+710) and Chicago Bears (+800) round out the top five.

There have been some early injuries shifting the tune in the NFC West. Los Angeles will be without star pass rusher Myles Garrett for at least the next month after placing him on Injured Reserve. Of course, Aaron Donald has yet to play as well. Sam Darnold is dealing with a hip injury and will also be out, making Drew Lock the starter for the upcoming weeks.

The 49ers have dealt with their mass of injuries already, with players like Ricky Pearsall and Alfred Collins set to miss the season, but their core group of stars was all healthy for Week 1.

San Francisco will first face the Seahawks on the road in Week 5 after three straight home games against the Miami Dolphins, Arizona Cardinals, and Denver Broncos. That could be the next major game that shifts the division odds one way or another, and could also be around when Sam Darnold returns.

item.title: NFL news, live updates: Ravens WR Ja'Kobi Lane reportedly out about 4 weeks; in Josh Jacobs case, motion made to keep video sealed
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news ahead of Week 2.
item.content:encoded:
That's a wrap on Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season. The Kansas City Chiefs ran all over the Denver Broncos for a 31-10 win on Monday night to close out the first week of regular-season action, with Kenneth Walker III leading the way in his debut for KC.

Among the biggest risers in our Week 2 NFL power rankings are the San Francisco 49ers, who climbed 11 spots after handily defeating the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 in their season opener in Australia. The Rams' pain didn't end with their Week 1 beating by the 49ers, either, as they'll be without DE Myles Garrett for at least four games after he had to undergo a knee procedure.

Some players who were injured in Week 1 have hope they will be back for Week 2, like Ladd McConkey of the Los Angeles Chargers. The wide receiver exited Sunday's loss to the Arizona Cardinals with a rib injury. Head coach Jim Harbaugh labeled him day-to-day. Zay Flowers left the Baltimore Ravens' game with a hamstring issue. He, too, is day-to-day and his injury is reportedly not considered serious. Teammate Ja’Kobi Lane, however, is reportedly out for about a month with a wrist injury.

In off-field news, the woman in Josh Jacobs’ case reportedly wants evidence permanently sealed, which could prevent the NFL from reviewing surveillance video. The evidence in the case involving the Green Bay Packers running back was then temporarily sealed, according to a Tuesday ESPN report, which details how the attorneys representing Jacobs' former girlfriend have filed a motion to permanently seal it as well as discovery materials.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more coming out of Week 1.

item.title: Cowboys positional rankings reveal where accountability needs to start
item.description: Last week was pretty frustrating.
item.content:encoded:
For me it’s quite simple: Because the expectations for the offense and defense were quite high, and both units were outcoached and outplayed by the Giants, the accountability falls squarely on Brian Schottenheimer and Christian Parker.

Alas, if only simple answers were the right answers – they almost never are.

  • The Cowboys went from two red-flag performances retained from the entire 2025 season to 12 in one game.
  • And perhaps even more strikingly, the team went from 13 starter-quality performances retained or acquired from 2025 to just four against the Giants.
  • This wasn’t simply a bad game. It was a remarkable concentration of bad individual performances.

One of the team captains, Quinnen Williams, has spoken up and announced the team would take accountability.

The idea today is to look at positional rankings (or percentile rankings) to identify which players and units need to take a little more constructive criticism than others. We’ve covered positional rankings extensively this offseason, go here if you need a quick primer.

The idea is that instead of using a player’s raw PFF Grade, we look at where a given player is ranked relative to the other players in the league at his position.

Relative positional performance gives us a way to separate the players who actually hurt the Cowboys from those who merely looked bad because the team lost.

Example: Jalen Thompson has a 43.7 Grade for the season opener, which suggests he had a slightly below-average game. But he ranks 71 out of 84 qualifying safeties, which would give him a positional ranking (1 – position rank / total qualifying players) * 100 of just 15, an indication of a red flag or bottom 20 performance.

Based on the overall ranking scale provided by PFF, the results can be split into quintiles, which delivers the following positional ranking groups:

The Good. Somewhat surprisingly, the Cowboys had more blue-chip performances on Sunday Night, than they had over the course of last year’s regular season. Moving into the blue chip quintile are Otito Ogbonnia (96),
Donovan Ezeiruaku (94), Javonte Williams (91), Tyler Booker (87), Cobie Durant (81) and rookie Jaishawn Barham (80), with Quinnen Williams (91) the only repeater from last year.

The Bad. The issue is that the team didn’t have enough starter quality performances (green) against the Giants, and replaced them with way too many red flag performances. Two players dropped from blue to red (George Pickens (95->9), Ryan Flournoy (88->1), three players (Jalen Thompson 67->15, James Houston 62->4, DeMarvion Overshown 65->0) fell directly from ‘green’ to ‘red’ and must count as the biggest disappointments from Sunday. Prescott ranks seventh out of 32 QBs at PFF, fourth out of 32 QBs in EPA/Play at rbsdm.com and third out of 32 in ESPN’s QBR.

Against the Giants, these players did not look like the reinforcements the Cowboys thought they were getting.

The Rookies: Four rookies made their NFL debut on Sunday, and as a group, they averaged a position rank of 50, which is better than the team average of 42, and which comes despite a forgettable performance from Malachi Lawrence.

The rookies weren’t the problem. Barham’s 80 and Downs’ 69 are particularly encouraging, especially considering the overall team average of 42.

Minimum to qualify in position ranks. For those interested, the Week 1 qualifying minimums are 10 snaps for all defenders and offensive linemen, 10 dropbacks for the QB, three targets for wide receivers, five targets for running backs, and no minimums for tight ends.

Last year, Kenneth Murray ranked 106 out of 108 qualifying linebackers, a position rank of just two. And even though it was plain to even the most cursory fan that Murray was a defensive liability, the Cowboys hung on to him, started him in 16 games and had him play 870 defensive snaps. The reasons remain unclear, was it because they thought they had no alternatives, was it because of stubborn coaches, was it because of the team’s belief in the sunk cost fallacy, was it because of the general Cowboys inertia when it comes to change? Who knows.

But we can’t have a repeat of that in 2026.

If the Cowboys really are going to be accountable, there have to be significant play-time adjustments for game two. In some cases, disappointing performances may be explainable as a one-off, but you can’t just go back to the drawing board and say, better communication, more assignment-sound play, fewer penalties and stuff like that will be enough to beat the Commanders next week. But better football and better players will.

If the positional rankings are telling us something real, the Cowboys need to respond to them with playing-time decisions. The injuries to Malik Hooker and DeMarvion Overshown already provide an opportunity for some personnel and playing-time changes, more playing-time changes elsewhere should be coming..

You can’t preach your way out of a bottom-five performance. At some point, accountability has to show up on the depth chart.

item.title: Our offense vs. their defense: Baltimore Ravens
item.description: Previewing the Saints’ offensive matchup in week 2
item.content:encoded:
After one week of NFL football being back, the New Orleans Saints currently sit with a record of 0-1 following their 31-30 loss to the Detroit Lions. Attention will now shift to another road matchup, this time versus the Baltimore Ravens, who are coming off of a 41-23 win over the Indianapolis Colts.

The Saints will enter week two as the fourth-ranked offense in the league after gaining 469 total yards. They accumulated 378 passing yards (1st in the league) and 91 rushing yards (22nd in the league) during last Sunday’s slate.

QB Tyler Shough leads both New Orleans and the NFL with 410 yards through the air even after throwing two interceptions and being sacked five times. Former Jacksonville Jaguar RB Travis Etienne Jr. led the Saints with 46 rushing yards, averaging just over five per carry. WR Chris Olave is also league-leading after his career-high 182 receiving yards on ten receptions even though he was kept out of the endzone by Detroit.

Size in the passing game led to majority of the Saints’ scoring after WR Devaughn Vele and TEs Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant hauled in touchdowns. RB Kendre Miller punched in the other New Orleans TD on the ground.

Meanwhile, the Baltimore defense is currently ranked sixth overall in the league after giving up just 251 yards of offense in week one. The Ravens allowed 149 yards through the air (5th in the league) and 102 yards rushing (13th in the league) in their first outing.

Ravens LB Roquan Smith had a team-leading 11 tackles versus the Colts and secured an interception. CB Marlon Humphrey came up with the only other turnover for Baltimore after forcing and recovering a fumble. Safety Malaki Starks and LB Tavius Robinson earned sacks last weekend for the Ravens and combined for 17 total yards tackled for a loss.

Baltimore’s defense held the Colts to just 16 points through three quarters before giving up a garbage time score. The Raven defense can play hardnosed, competitive football long into the game meaning New Orleans will not be able to rely on too many late heroics and scoring spurts if they want any shot of getting their record up to .500 and avoiding an 0-2 start.

item.title: Week 1 AP NFL Power Rankings: Chiefs make their debut in the top 5
item.description: The Arrowhead Pride team ranks the National Football League from top to bottom.
item.content:encoded:
Was this the best Week 1 of an NFL season in recent memory?

Normally, the opening week brings sloppy play across the league, as many teams don’t play their starters in the preseason. We are used to seeing offenses struggle to get into sync, with defenses having the advantage early in the season. That wasn’t the case in this weekend’s slate of games.

Fantasy football managers rejoiced as we saw an offensive explosion across the league. Is this a sign of a historic offensive season upcoming, or will defenses eventually catch up?

Some things looked different, but others stayed the same.

The NFC South is 0-4. The Cleveland Browns are still the Browns. And oh yeah, Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes is healthy, and the AFC West runs through Arrowhead.

Like the Chiefs’ running game, the Arrowhead Pride NFL Power Rankings are back this season.

This week, along with me, staff voters were Maurice Elston, Caleb James, Ron Kopp Jr., Rocky Magana, Jared Sapp, and Matt Stagner.

1. Seattle Seahawks

No Sam Darnold? No problem. The defending champs still looked like the champs in their Super Bowl rematch.

2. Baltimore Ravens

Derrick Henry defies all odds of a normal human being. 

3. Buffalo Bills

Josh Allen has a way of putting his team on his back and playing like Superman. And if his defense keeps playing as they did in Week 1, he’ll have to be Superman every week.

4. San Francisco 49ers

This is why we play the games. Seemingly, not much went right for the 49ers this offseason. Written off as the “has-been” in the NFC West. Yet, they dominated in Melbourne. Their travel plan couldn’t have been better.

5. Kansas City Chiefs

I don’t know about you, but that was the most fun I’ve had watching the Chiefs since 2023. I wanted to reach through the television and give Kenneth Walker a hug.

6. Cincinnati Bengals

The new Bengals? Usually slow starters, they start 2026 with a victory. Their defense looked new and improved, but their franchise stars, Burrow and Chase, played a lackluster game.

7. Houston Texans

This Texans’ defense did not live up to their “historic” billing. Superman gave them two turnover opportunities in the second half, but they couldn’t capitalize. CJ Stroud looked like he’s playing for that new contract this season.

8. Chicago Bears

Head coach Ben Johnson said his goal for the Bears is to be the top-scoring offense in league history. He wants shutouts and blowouts. He got the blowout, and they’re on track for that scoring record. However, they’ve got some work to do on that defense if we’re going to see some shutouts in the Windy City.

9. Philadelphia Eagles

Anyone else thrilled the Tush Push didn’t show up on Sunday?

10. Jacksonville Jaguars

Such a sneaky team who could be a sleeper in the AFC. Is Trevor Lawrence a dark horse MVP candidate?

11. Los Angeles Rams

The NFL’s offseason darlings were flat-out embarrassed on Friday Thursday night in Australia. Hindsight is 20/20, but I guess it wasn’t a great idea to get off a 16-hour flight and play a football game.

12. Denver Broncos

Personally, I can’t wait for the Broncos to (over)pay Bo Nix.

13. Detroit Lions

About as disheartening an overtime victory as you can get. The Lions were a Saints’ failed two-point conversion in overtime away from letting a 21-0 lead slip through their fingers.

14. New England Patriots

Yikes. Not going to win many football games if your franchise quarterback throws three interceptions in the fourth quarter.

15. New York Giants

I’m just trying to imagine John Harbaugh and Cam Skattebo having a conversation. Regardless, this is an exciting young team to watch. They could make a run back to the postseason.

16. Minnesota Vikings

Kyler Murray’s Vikings debut didn’t last long. Wily vet Carson Wentz saved the day with a big comeback win over the Pack. QB controversy in Minnesota?

17. Green Bay Packers

Is the seat starting to get warm for Matt Lafleur in Green Bay?

18. Pittsburgh Steelers

Aaron Rodgers is louder off the field than he is on it these days.

19. Dallas Cowboys

More of the same from them. This defense didn’t look any better.

20. Los Angeles Chargers

LOL. Chargers gonna Charger.

21. Tampa Bay Buccaneers

After dusting himself off from getting sacked four times, Baker’s first thought has to be his revenge game against the Cleveland Browns.

22. Arizona Cardinals

The team that knocked you out of your Survivor League before it got started.

23. New Orleans Saints

Is Shough enough? There will be highs and lows with him, but such a fun player to watch. He almost completed the remarkable comeback in the Motor City.

24. Indianapolis Colts

That’s an awful defensive performance for a team who has invested so heavily in that unit.

25. Washington Commanders

Stefon Diggs is continuing his antics in a new city.

26. Carolina Panthers

The Panthers have quietly put up 37 and 31 points in their two most recent showings, dating back to the Wild Card Round of last year’s playoffs. Although both games were losses, is this a sign of things to come for the Panthers’ offense?

27. Las Vegas Raiders

Ashton Jeanty is a scary running back. Reminder that the Raiders also started 1-0 last season. But they’ve got talent.

28. Atlanta Falcons

The NFC South is 0-4 to start the 2026 season. Perhaps no team exemplifies the South more than the Falcons. Some of the most elite offensive talent in the league—except at the most important position on the field.

29. New York Jets

The Jets got the win, but a single interception remains elusive.

30. Miami Dolphins

I challenge any NFL fan to name five players on this roster. They are in complete rebuild mode. 

31. Tennessee Titans

Will the Titans have a new stadium and quarterback in 2027? Cam Ward didn’t look great in the season opener.

32. Cleveland Browns

Is there a fan base in the NFL you feel worse for? It would just feel impossible to be a Browns fan.

item.content:encoded:
Hello Chicago Bears Fans!  Welcome to my in-season series on the striped ones, the zebras, the arbiters-of-the-yellow-flag, that’s right – the refs.  Every week when the Bears end up in the loss column, Bears fans leave Soldier Field (or the living room) with the same two questions: Did we actually lose that game, or did the officials take it from us?  And when we are in the win column, we will inevitably hear from opponents’ fans that they were robbed by the refs.  Well, were they?  Upon Further Review exists to answer these questions with film, the rulebook, and a consistent grading scale: Each week I’ll isolate the flags and no-calls that went against Chicago and against the opponent, grade every one as Correct, Arguable, Incorrect, or Horrible, then roll those grades into four numbers: a Calls-Against-Bears rating, a Calls-Against-Opponent rating, an overall referee performance score, and a differential that shows which sideline got the better of the crew. I’ll also pull the most controversial calls from around the league so we can see what call this year will have NFL fans screaming, “wait, what?” and NFL rules analysts assuring us, “always has been.”

Chicago beat Carolina 59–37 on Sunday in Charlotte. Official totals: Bears 12 penalties for 57 yards, Panthers 11 for 84 yards. Below are all accepted flags, in order, with the player named, the yardage, the game clock, and the score when the penalty was enforced.

First Quarter

  • Rome Odunze (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 15:00, first play from scrimmage. Swift’s 17-yard run came back; ball spotted at the CHI 19.
  • Dayo Odeyingbo (CHI), roughing the passer, 1 yard — 12:54. After Young’s 26-yard completion to Coker at the CHI 2. Half-the-distance; first-and-goal at the 1.
  • Montez Sweat (CHI), defensive offside, 0 yards — 12:44. Already at the 1; replay first-and-goal.
  • Darren Waller (CAR), offensive pass interference, 9 yards — 12:29. Waller’s 1-yard TD catch wiped off. First-and-goal from the 10.

CHI 0, CAR 7

  • Garrett Bradbury (CHI), offensive holding, 9 yards — 10:09. Swift’s 9-yard run on 3rd-and-1 nullified.
  • Cairo Santos (CHI), kickoff short of landing zone — 5:52. Ball placed at the CAR 40 (no yardage in the official 57-yard total).

CHI 14, CAR 7

  • Isaiah Simmons (CAR), offensive holding, 10 yards — 1:59, on the kickoff return. Carolina started at its 17.
  • M. Freeling (CAR), false start, 5 yards — 1:27.

Second Quarter

CHI 14, CAR 7

  • Mitchell Evans (CAR), unnecessary roughness, 15 yards — 15:00. After Raymond’s 23-yard punt return to the CHI 44; Bears started at the CAR 41 and scored two plays later (Kmet 22-yard TD).

CHI 21, CAR 14

  • S. Thomas (CHI), illegal block above the waist, 10 yards — 12:40, on the kickoff return. Bears started at their 12.
  • Dayo Odeyingbo (CHI), illegal use of hands, 2 yards — 9:21. Half-the-distance; first-and-goal at the 2. Carolina later scored on Young’s 7-yard scramble.
  • Carolina, illegal shift, 5 yards — 9:09. Wiped a 1-yard Hubbard run at the goal line.

CHI 24, CAR 21

  • James Lynch (CHI), defensive offside, 5 yards — 5:16.
  • Robert Hunt (CAR), offensive holding, 10 yards — 4:11. Brooks’ 12-yard run came back.

CHI 24, CAR 24

  • Chicago, delay of game, 5 yards — 0:38. Williams still converted and scored on a 29-yard scramble two plays later (31–24 at half).

Third Quarter

CHI 31, CAR 31

  • Colston Loveland (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 4:55. Created 2nd-and-20 at the CAR 21.
  • Derrick Brown (CAR), roughing the passer, 10 yards — 4:31. After Williams threw the ball away on that 2nd-and-20. Automatic first down at the CAR 11; Swift scored from the 1 three plays later (38–31).

CHI 38, CAR 31

  • Cairo Santos (CHI), kickoff short of landing zone — 3:05. Again spotted at the CAR 40.
  • R. Walker (CAR), false start, 5 yards — 2:33. Carolina then failed on 4th-and-3; Monangai ripped the 61-yard TD on the next snap (45–31).

Fourth Quarter

CHI 45, CAR 31

  • Chicago, illegal formation, 5 yards — 12:48.
  • Derrick Brown (CAR), defensive offside, 0 yards — 7:21. Nullified Bobby Brown III’s interception in the end zone. Williams threw a 1-yard TD to Jahdae Walker two plays later (52–31).

CHI 52, CAR 31

  • Jalen Coker (CAR), offensive pass interference, 10 yards — 4:38. Wiped a 1-yard TD pass to Mitchell Evans. Carolina still scored on Coker’s 8-yard catch; PAT blocked (52–37).
  • T. Gipson (CAR), neutral zone infraction, 5 yards — 3:52. Gifted Chicago a first down; Swift scored from 28 yards on the next play (59–37).

Snapshot: Flags For and Against

In our inaugural UFR, I’m glad I’m not in a position to analyze the flags that cost us the game.  In fact, it was flags against the Carolina Panthers that were pivotal – the first-ever “roughing the passer” call for Caleb Williams, erasing a 2nd and 20 near the red zone, and an interception at the goal line that was erased by an offside. Both of those flags were on Carolina Panthers defensive lineman, Derrick Brown. Carolina also had two touchdowns called back for offensive pass interference (Waller in Q1, Coker/Evans in Q4). That said, while those penalties were certainly the most impactful, in my evaluation none of them were incorrect calls. Chicago’s flags were more volume than impact—two landing-zone kickoffs, two holdings that were overcome, and a pair of small defensive infractions near the goal line—except Odeyingbo’s first-quarter roughing, which put Carolina at the 1, and arguably Rome Odunze’s holding call on the first snap of the game, which killed a first down run, and on the next play Luther Burden would fumble the football, leading to a Carolina touchdown.

Flag of the Game: The “Roughing the Passer” on Derrick Brown

Rule that matters: once the passer leaves the pocket and throws on the run, he loses the one-step protection. He still cannot be hit late with no attempt to avoid, stuffed, or driven through. Williams is outside the pocket, retreating, then dumps the ball toward the sideline. Brown (#95) is still coming. Contact is after the release. Williams goes down hard. Brown said he thought it was one step. Canales called it the two-step rule and “tight.”
From video review, it is more than one step. Both from a forcible contact perspective (forearm to Caleb’s sternum) and from the differential between when the pass left Caleb’s hand and when Brown made contact (close to two full steps) – this is classic RTP.  I rate this call correct.  Brown had plenty of time to pull up and instead he delivers a blow to the quarterback.

Upon Further Review — Week 1: Bears 59, Panthers 37
Crew: Brad Allen. Official totals: Chicago 12–57, Carolina 11–84.
Scale: Correct / Arguable / Incorrect / Horrible.
Weight is impact, not whether the flag was right: 1 housekeeping, 2 drive-changer, 3 scoring-situation / automatic first down that feeds points, 4 wiped score, wiped takeaway, or a dead drive flipped into a touchdown.

Calls Against Chicago


Calls against Carolina

Against CAR: 6 Correct, 5 Arguable, 0 Incorrect, 0 Horrible.

Calls against the Bears: 6/12 Correct (50%), 6 Arguable, none wrong. Quality: clean but busy. Chicago’s flags were mostly self-inflicted alignment, delay, and two landing-zone kicks. The two that actually fed Carolina points were Odeyingbo’s RTP and hands-to-the-face — both Arguable without All-22.

Calls against the opponent: 6/11 Correct (54.5%), 5 Arguable, none wrong. Quality: same gray, worse timing. Carolina’s book is full of dead-ball and alignment mistakes (false starts, offside, NZI) plus two wiped TDs and one wiped INT.

Total ref performance:12 Correct, 11 Arguable, 0 Incorrect, 0 Horrible on 23 accepted flags. No flag in the public record is egregious. Allen’s crew did not gift a phantom 15-yarder that the tape clearly kills. They did live in the judgment pile (holds, OPI, RTP) and arguably were overly litigious in littering the field with laundry on Sunday.

If you count only wrong calls, the differential is 0–0. The refs did not steal this game. If you count Correct Weight-4 results, Carolina beat themselves: the wiped INT and the NZI before the 28-yarder, and the key call – the RTP against Brown, are on the Panthers. If you count Arguable Weight-4 results, the ledger leans Chicago +4 impact points (Evans UR vs Waller OPI + Coker OPI, with Odeyingbo’s two red-zone flags on the other side).

Headline for the series: Brad Allen’s crew was sloppy in volume, but got the key calls right for the most part. The two flags that actually decided the second half were a bang-bang RTP that the rulebook confirms and an offside Brown owned in his postgame interview.

Grading the officials in the Bears-Panthers game: Picky but Correct.

Now, let’s talk about the most controversial call in the NFL over the weekend. Second quarter, Lions 7–0, about 9:34 left in the half. Detroit faced a long down (reports put it around 2nd-and-16) near its own 23. Jared Goff dropped to throw. Chase Young beat Penei Sewell, hit Goff as he wound up, and the ball came out backward, rolling toward the Lions’ 12. Jonas Sanker scooped it and scored. On the field it was a backward pass / live ball and a Saints touchdown that would have tied the game pending the PAT.

Replay took the points off. The ruling became an incomplete forward pass. Detroit punted instead of lining up to kick off after a 7–7 score. The Lions later won 31–30 in overtime.

What looked like a fumble was treated as a pass because of a specific rule, Rule 3, Section 21, Article 3, Item 1: if a defender materially affects the passer after the throwing motion has started, it is a forward pass no matter where the ball lands. “Throwing motion” starts when the passer begins to bring the ball up in the windup — not when the hand finishes moving forward. Mike Pereira said it on Fox: hand goes up, then he’s hit, intent was to throw forward, so it’s incomplete wherever it hits.

Mark Butterworth, the league’s VP of instant replay, put it in the pool report: if Young had hit Goff before that motion started, it could be a backward pass and a live fumble. Because the motion had already started, contact that sent the ball backward still made it a forward pass.

While this may be correct on the rule in some technical sense, there has never been a stronger consensus that this was a nonsense, obviously wrong, call than the social media reaction to it. Everyone saw a ball travel 10–15 yards behind the line and a scoop-and-score. Suggesting that Goff’s “intent” to throw the ball forward is determinative is a tough pill to swallow for any objective NFL football fan. Even Dan Campbell said he thought Detroit had lost the play live and “got one.”


For Upon Further Review: this is the Week 1 NFL Call of the Week.  You decide the grade and the significance of the call.

How would you grade it? And what do you think about how the officials did in the Panthers-Bears game?  Let us know in the comments below!

item.title: Broncos vs Jaguars preview: Denver looks to drastically improve
item.description: Bo Nix and the Broncos were just curb-stomped by the Chiefs. Denver will look to get back on track this Sunday in Week 2.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos were unmercifully flogged in their opener.

What makes it even tougher is that it came against a hated rival. Now the Broncos have to learn from this, improve, and get ready for another tough matchup this Sunday.

Teams face adversity, and Denver has that in spades early in the season. How do the Broncos respond? What improvements do they make against the Jacksonville Jaguars?

To add a little flavor to the mix, you have the result from last season’s game between these two teams when Denver got whopped by the Jaguars in Week 16, 34-20.

FanDuel Sportsbook currently has the Broncos as the -2.5-point home favorites on Sunday. The total sits at 45.5, with a lean towards the under at -115.

Offensive Rankings 

Jacksonville: Fourteenth in total offense (360 yards per game), 11th in rushing offense (126 YPG), 10th in passing offense (234 YPG), sixth in scoring offense (34 points per game).

Denver: Thirty-second in total offense (176 yards per game), 31st in rushing offense (61 YPG), 32nd in passing offense (115 YPG), tied for 28th in scoring offense (10 points per game).

Defensive Rankings   

Jacksonville: Tenth in total defense (272 yards per game), ninth in rushing defense (87 YPG), tied for 13th in passing defense (185 YPG), tied for second in scoring defense (10 points per game).

Denver: Twenty-fourth in total defense (392 yards per game), 31st in rushing defense (220 YPG), 10th in passing defense (172 YPG), tied for 23rd in scoring defense (31 points per game).

Here are the MHR staff’s keys to Sunday’s game.

Do the opposite of whatever Denver just did

Whatever the hell we witnessed in Kansas City, the Broncos must do the complete opposite against Jacksonville. That starts by looking and playing like an NFL team. For Denver to do that, it needs to really hammer down the preparation this week. Bo Nix called the loss to the Chiefs “an ugly wake-up call.” Here’s hoping the Broncos got the message and don’t hit the snooze button. Come together as a team, do the little things, limit the costly mistakes, and execute. — Ian St. Clair

Tackle!

Watching Kenneth Walker embarrass the Broncos defense was eye-opening. Patrick Mahomes constantly escaping on that reconstructed knee was baffling. It wasn’t that the defense played horribly; it just found ways to miss tackles, making it impossible to win. If Denver can’t wrap up the Jaguars, mark down 0-2 and a major uphill climb to the playoffs. — Adam Malnati

Better play on third down

The Broncos struggled to stop the Chiefs on third down on Monday Night Football. Moreover, they kept shooting themselves in the foot on offense and were dreadful in that aspect. This was also an issue for them last December, when they lost to the Jacksonville Jaguars. If they can’t do better at extending drives or getting off the field in key situations, they’ll continue to be their own worst enemies. Their performance in these situations has to get better to be successful. — Christopher Hart

Better offensive game plan

We need to make sure the Jaguars don’t coat themselves in oil, making it impossible for our defenders to tackle them as the Chiefs did. Seriously, though, we need a better offensive game plan to counter what the Jags will do on defense. The Bronco offense looked completely unprepared for the funky blitz packages that Spags always uses. Also, the Broncos need to do a better job of convincing the refs not to call holding on them when they are blatantly holding. The Broncos should ask the Chiefs what their secret is. — Joe Mahoney

Score more points than the other team

Data and analytics tell you that the Broncos are winless when they score less than their opponent and are undefeated when they score more. So, the game plan is simple! Score more points than the Jaguars. You didn’t do that against the Chiefs, and we’re all angry and disappointed. Do that vs. the small-market Jags, and we’ll be happy again. — Scotty Payne

What are your keys to Sunday’s game?

item.title: Seahawks power rankings roundup: Seahawks stay on top, Rams slip from national glory
item.description: Despite an injury to Sam Darnold, the national media is still high on the Super Bowl champions.
item.content:encoded:
Entering the 2026 season, the national media has been very high on the Seattle Seahawks. This is not surprising as the team just won the Super Bowl, and in a dominant way. Across the NFL landscape, the consensus top two teams appeared to be the Seahawks and their division rival, Los Angeles Rams. However, will the national media keep the Seahawks in a top position with their win over the New England Patriots? Or will the loss of Sam Darnold to a glute injury show them slip in the rankings? Let’s take a look at five national media sites power rankings (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (B/R), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle. 

Starting with the bad news … if you can call it bad. ESPN ranks the Seahawks at number two in the NFL, keeping the same ranking they had entering the season. In this ranking ESPN notes that rookie running back Jadarian Price had a solid debut, while also  giving a shoutout to safety, Rodney Thomas II who played for an injured Ty Okada. The only team ranked above Seattle was the Buffalo Bills. 

Entering the season, both CBS Sports and PFT had the Seahawks ranked as the number one team in the league. Their win over the Patriots did not change this. In their ranking, CBS Sports shows optimism that Seattle can keep winning with backup quarterback, Drew Lock at the helm. On the opposite end of the spectrum, despite keeping the Seahawks ranked at number one, PFT does question how long the team can keep winning with Drew Lock at the helm. 

Neither NFL.com nor B/R had the Seahawks ranked number one entering the 2026 season. However, after the week one victory over the Patriots, both have moved Seattle into the top spot. The biggest jump was with NFL.com, who originally had the Seahawks ranked number three entering the season. In this week’s ranking, NFL.com moved them up to number one on the list, and highlighted the team’s big second half comeback, led by three fourth-quarter takeaways, and a signature Jaxon Smith-Njigba touchdown. 

B/R on the other hand moved the Seahawks up from second to first. In this ranking, B/R notes that this team’s victory with Drew Lock at quarterback shows just how dominant of a team they are. An added note that B/R made was that the “Seahawks should’ve been No.1 to start out power rankings.” The team that Seattle took the top spot away from? The Los Angeles Rams – who have now fallen to sixth in BR’s rankings. 

I know this is a Seahawks power rankings roundup. However, it is sweet to see the Rams fall from national grace. It isn’t just BR who dropped the Rams down a lot in their rankings. ESPN also had the Rams falling from first entering the season to being ranked fourth. NFL.com dropped the Rams from first to seventh. CBS Sports dropped the Rams from second to fifth. And lastly, PFT had the Rams drop all the way from second to 11th. 

Overall, the Seahawks have to be feeling good after pulling off that come from behind victory with a backup quarterback, first time play-caller, and with it all being week one of the season (and banner night of all nights). The national media feels good about the team as well. Entering the season the average power ranking between the five polled sites was 1.8. This week the average power ranking between the five sites is 1.2. Although it is small, this still shows an upward trend. 

Despite going into next week with backup, Drew Lock, the Seahawks are still likely going to be favorites against the Arizona Cardinals. However, this is the NFL, and if Seattle is caught slipping, they may very well see a similar fall in rankings as the Rams did this past week.

item.title: The Giants showed they can be ‘dangerous’, will the Rams?
item.description: Matthew Stafford calls the New York Giants “dangerous”, and plenty more NFL news on a Wednesday!
item.content:encoded:
Matthew Stafford referred to the New York Giants as a “dangerous” football team, and he further explained that every team in the NFL has a chance to be dangerous. The logic that any team can be dangerous makes sense as every team is made up of the best talent in the world. So, by extension, the Los Angeles Rams can be dangerous too, right?

One would think, but it’s hard not to be a little concerned or maybe more than a little concerned given how disappointing they were in Week 1. Now, Myles Garrett is out too.

For the Giants, we just saw them be very dangerous over a touted Dallas Cowboys team on Sunday Night Football. The Giants showed they had the goods in Week 1. They’ll look to do it again in Week 2.

It’s not all doom and gloom, it’s one week. But the Rams haven’t shown, so far, that they have the goods to be a dangerous team for four quarters in 2026. Will they find that gear on Monday night?

Tune in, find out.

Matthew Stafford shares early thoughts on ‘dangerous’ Giants (ramswire)

“Obviously, the young quarterback, Jaxson Dart, I thought played really well, played within himself, made some plays with his feet,” he added. “They’re a dangerous team. I think every team in the NFL, it’s what people out there forget, year in and year out going through training camps and watching preseason, think they can pick who’s gonna win every game. And that’s why we play them. You put the ball down, you go play the games. And I thought the Giants did a heck of a job the other night. I thought it was cool on the weekend of September 11th, 25 years later, for the Giants in New York City to get a win, felt right and felt great to have the NFL have something like that happen and those guys play well.”

NFL power rankings Week 2: There’s a new No. 1 after Rams tumble (usatoday)

“Seattle Seahawks (2): Should’ve known they’d demand and command the respect of a reigning champion that deserves the No. 1 slot until proven otherwise. Did the ‘Hawks look spectacular while winning their Super Bowl rematch with the Patriots, despite losing QB Sam Darnold five plays in to a hip injury? Nope. Did they show their typical grit and dominant defense while again vanquishing a quality opponent? Yep. And plenty of upward mobility, as they’ll tell you. “We’ll improve our operation,” said coach Mike Macdonald after the win. “(W)e can get so much better very quickly.” Good bet they will.”

How did former Rams OLB Jared Verse play in his Browns debut? (ramswire)

“Similar to Garrett’s first game with the Rams, Verse’s debut with the Browns was disappointing. He finished the game with four tackles, one of which went for a loss, but zero sacks or quarterback hits. According to Pro Football Focus, Verse didn’t record a single pressure and also missed one tackle.”

Why Richard Sherman is concerned about Rams’ defense, and it has nothing to do with Myles Garrett injury (clutchpoints)

“The corners you got are great corners, but they have played in (Steve Spagnuolo’s) system their whole career, and you don’t run to Spags’ defense…You don’t use a Corvette to Uber. You get in a Corvette, you’re racing…you pay them their money, let him do what he was doing,” he said, per Kevin Clark on X, formerly Twitter.

Sherman wasn’t the only one to question how the Rams utilized new cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson in their season opener, as Brock Purdy and the 49ers’ offense seemed to have no issues moving the ball down the field throughout the evening.“

Matthew Stafford downplays Rams’ big injury as ‘little bump in the road’ before four-game gauntlet (nypost)

““This is just a blip in the radar, a little bump in the road,” Stafford said on the “Let’s Go!” podcast, predicting Garrett would work diligently to return quickly.

Stafford understands the expectations attached to a blockbuster acquisition, having arrived under similar pressure in 2021. He also emphasized that Garrett is “a human being, too” and said the entire team must compensate for his absence.“

Another baby girl is joining the Rams ‘Ramily’ after star player’s heartwarming Instagram announcement (nypost)

“Terrance Ferguson’s second NFL season may have started quietly, but away from the football field, the Los Angeles Rams tight end just received much bigger news. 

Ferguson and his wife, Sophia, announced Tuesday that they are expecting their first child, a baby girl, in early 2027.

The couple shared the news on Instagram with a photograph featuring a pink Nike baby outfit, tiny pink Air Jordans, a pregnancy test, an ultrasound photo and a sign reading, “Baby Ferguson coming 2027.” Their two dogs completed the family portrait wearing matching pink bandanas declaring, “It’s a girl.”

NFL Power Rankings, Week 2: Seahawks leapfrog Broncos and Rams into No. 1 spot; Chiefs hit top 10 (nfl.com)

“Week 1 is complete, and as is always the case with the opening weekend of a new season, surprises appeared all over the place. 

The Cardinals rolled into SoFi Stadium, punched the Chargers in the mouth, stole their lunch money and ran back to the desert cackling with satisfaction. The Saints nearly pulled off a legendary comeback in Detroit. And for yet another year, we learned it was unwise to trust the hype surrounding the Cowboys.

Who climbed? Who fell? And which of these movers will age poorly in a month’s time? Let’s rank all 32!

NOTE: Up/down arrows below reflect movement from the Week 1 edition of the Power Rankings.“

Gimme Him: One player New York Giants would steal from Los Angeles Rams (giantswire)

“The Giants currently have a cornerback room consisting of Deonte Banks, Greg Newsome II, Paulson Adebo, and Dru Phillips as the main contributors. McDuffie is far and away the best player out of that group.

The 2023 All-Pro First-Team selection has allowed a career 89.1 passer rating against and a mere 6.0 yards per target in coverage. Though this scenario is hypothetical, it goes to show that the Giants are likely to address the cornerback position in a big way this offseason.

What do you say, Giants fans? Would you steal McDuffie from the Rams or go in an entirely different direction?“

Giants vs. Rams Prediction, Odds, Spread, Injuries, Trends for NFL Week 2 (si.com)

“It was a disastrous Week 1 for the Los Angeles Rams. They flew all the way to Australia only to get crushed by their divisional rival, the San Francisco 49ers, 27-7. Not only that, but they’ve had to put their new defensive acquisition, Myles Garrett, on IR.

The Super Bowl favorites now need to bounce back in a hurry and will hope to do so in Week 2 on Monday Night Football when they host the New York Giants.“

The 49ers get the top spot because their win was a division win. The Cardinals have the edge over Seattle, thanks to a greater point differential. The Rams, well, they are 0-1.“

IF Turner and/ or Young are true FRANCHISE defensive players worthy of $30+ million a year…. they should not NEED Garrett and AD to be an above-average defense.

If you call for a defense of Garrett and AD…. they already have that (according to pundits) with Young and Turner… younger versions of the guys”-PAramsfan1972

The Los Angeles Rams losing a weird game in Australia, for which they gambled that an aggressive travel plan wouldn't affect them but were obviously wrong, isn't that bad. They played terribly but it's fine to excuse it to having to play across the world.

But then, after not posting a single stat in a quiet Rams debut, Myles Garrett said his knee wasn't feeling well. A few days later, it was reported that Garrett was having knee surgery. On Monday, Rams head coach Sean McVay said there's no timetable for Garrett's return. He'll be out at least four weeks on injured reserve.

That can't be ignored as easily.

The Rams came into the season as the clear Super Bowl favorite, and that's already in question. It's not just losing Garrett, the best defensive player in the NFL. Matthew Stafford is 38 and he looked awful in the opener. When Rich Gannon won his first NFL MVP at age 37, like Stafford did last season, he threw only nine touchdowns the rest of his career. The age cliff finds everyone. Davante Adams, at 33, was a non-factor in the opener against the 49ers. The defense around Garrett didn't play well. Maybe it was all Australia. Maybe not.

Going forward without Garrett for however long is scary for this defense. The Rams had to trade Jared Verse to Cleveland in the Garrett deal, so they now have a big hole at defensive end. Aaron Donald being a force after returning from two years off is a lot more questionable without Garrett around to command double teams. The 49ers gained 379 yards and had no problems in the air or on the ground. Again, maybe that's just fatigue from a long trip, but we don't know yet. We also don't know if the long trip will impact the Rams for a few weeks to come. The Rams face the Giants on Monday night in Week 2, and that matchup doesn't look so easy after the Giants played well in their opening-game win against the Cowboys.

It's typically not a good idea to overreact to Week 1. The Raiders won at New England in last season's opener. Las Vegas went 3-14 and the Patriots went 14-3. Weird things happen in the beginning. However, there should be concern about the Rams. Not enough to send them way down the rankings, but enough that their standing as the clear Super Bowl favorite, or even the favorite in the NFC West, is in question. It's a top-heavy team and there are significant worries about their stars just one week into the season. We might not get a clear picture of who the Rams are until Garrett returns and shows he's back to his normal self. Whenever that will be.

Here are the NFL power rankings after Week 1 of the NFL season:

32. Miami Dolphins (0-1, Last week: 32)

Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said success wouldn't be defined by wins or losses but development, and while he got a hard time for saying it, it's true for the 2026 Dolphins. In that way, it was good to see rookies like linebacker Jacob Rodriguez (a game-high 14 tackles and he played all 68 defensive snaps) and receiver Caleb Douglas (five catches, 94 yards) play well. This team still has a significantly insufficient roster, hence why it is in this spot even though it didn't embarrass itself like the …

31. Tennessee Titans (0-1, LW: 27)

An argument can be made that the Titans deserve to be No. 32. No team looked worse in Week 1. Against a Jets team that was 3-14 last season, the Titans had seven first downs and three points before their final possession, when they trailed by 20 points. Tennessee forced one punt and zero turnovers in the first three quarters. If you get dominated by the Jets at home, it could be a very long season. It probably explains the booing that fans gave the Titans. "When you lose, you're a loser," head coach Robert Saleh bluntly said afterward, acknowledging the discontent. Could more be on the immediate horizon? Up next for the Titans is a home game against the Eagles.

30. Cleveland Browns (0-1, LW: 30)

The Browns' defense is supposed to keep them in games, even with Jared Verse replacing Myles Garrett. That wasn't the case in the opener as the Browns looked like they really missed Jim Schwartz as defensive coordinator. Trevor Lawrence had four touchdowns and Jacksonville had 31 points with 12:08 left in the third quarter. If Cleveland's defense is bad, there's no hope at a respectable season.

29. Atlanta Falcons (0-1, LW: 28)

It's hard to get too excited about the start of the season when Cooper Rush is QB1. Head coach Kevin Stefanski gave no update Monday on who'll be the starter for Week 2 vs. the Panthers. Michael Penix Jr. might return soon, but will that fix much? Atlanta's defense played well in the Falcons' loss at Pittsburgh, but that probably has more to do with the Steelers' offense that was held to 3-of-13 on third downs and 0-for-2 on fourth. Despite the quagmire everywhere around him, Bijan Robinson still managed 83 rushing yards and 90 receiving yards. So there, Falcons fans have one reason to be excited.

28. Arizona Cardinals (1-0, LW: 31)

It shouldn't be a surprise that the Cardinals looked good on offense. Their quarterback situation isn't ideal but they have good skill position players. The surprise of their season-opening upset win was Arizona's defense. The Chargers got just 268 yards, they sacked Justin Herbert three times and had an interception and fumble recovery. Andrew Wingard, who had the interception of Herbert, had something he partially got off his chest postgame. "Everyone has been trashing this defense, trashing coach [Nick] Rallis," Wingard said of his defensive coordinator. "It's like … I'm going to be polite and not say what I want to say, but — it's not gratifying because it'd only be gratifying if you cared about it, but I'm just happy for all these guys." Arizona was eighth in EPA (expected points added) allowed per play through Sunday's Week 1 games. The Cardinals were projected to have one of the NFL's worst defenses this season, but that wasn't the case in the opener. A matchup against the Seahawks now looks more interesting.

27. New York Jets (1-0, LW: 29)

We'll likely look back at the Jets' Week 1 win and realize the Titans really are that bad. However, allowing 195 yards to any NFL team is impressive. The Jets gained 367 yards and generally looked sharp in all ways on offense. Head coach Aaron Glenn needs to show improvement this season and he's off to a great start, even if it was against Tennessee.

26. Carolina Panthers (0-1, LW: 25)

The focus was on the Bears' offense, but the Panthers' defense was part of that story. Carolina had never allowed more than 52 points in a game before allowing 59 on Sunday. The Panthers spent big on the defense in the offseason and the results for Week 1 were awful. They wasted a fantastic performance by Bryce Young, who had 361 yards and three touchdowns passing and rushed for another score. Defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero might be on the hot seat early this season. "Like I said, it's embarrassing, but ultimately, I'm taking a really positive outlook from this because we can only get better from here," Panthers outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips said, via the team's site.

25. Las Vegas Raiders (1-0, LW: 26)

The Raiders can thank the schedule makers. Getting Miami at home to start the season was great for a team that had so many changes, including a new head coach in Klint Kubiak. They still had to execute no matter the opponent and the Raiders did just that, winning 27-13. It was without tight end Brock Bowers, who will hopefully be back soon from a meniscus trim in his knee. It was a good start, though the Raiders had a good start last season with a win at New England. This time they have to build on it.

24. Indianapolis Colts (0-1, LW: 19)

Daniel Jones returning for Week 1, a little more than nine months after tearing his Achilles, always felt aggressive. And Jones didn't play well in Week 1. He was 28th among 30 qualified quarterbacks in adjusted EPA per play through Sunday's Week 1 games. Pair that with a defense that allowed 506 yards to the Ravens, and there should be plenty of concern in Indianapolis after just one game.

23. New Orleans Saints (0-1, LW: 24)

The Saints have a rightful complaint that a defensive touchdown was taken off the board due to a convoluted explanation of why Jared Goff's pass that went backward was actually incomplete. With that play, the Saints probably win a game that they eventually lost in overtime. Still, being a 2-point conversion away from beating a talented Lions team on the road is a positive sign for the season.

22. Washington Commanders (0-1, LW: 22)

Everything was labored with Jayden Daniels and the Commanders' offense. The line didn't protect well but Daniels often held the ball too long, perhaps because his receivers weren't getting open. He averaged 3.41 seconds per throw, the slowest among all QBs through Sunday's games, per Next Gen Stats. (H/T to reporter Tashan Reed for pointing that out.) The Eagles have a good defense and that led to some of the issues. But the opener wasn't a good omen, especially for new coordinator David Blough. At least he has Daniels in his corner. The QB defended the shovel pass play that the Eagles stuffed on a 2-point conversion attempt, preventing a tie in the final minute of regulation. "It was the right call," Daniels told reporters postgame. "Anything Blough calls, man. I'm with him. Regardless, however everybody else might want to view it, man, I'm with Blough 100%."

21. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-1, LW: 21)

The Buccaneers played well enough to win at the Bengals but they turned it over four times, one of which was returned for a touchdown and another that came at the Bengals' 4-yard line. You can't ignore that because it's a continuation of the sloppiness that cost the Bucs a division title last season. The good news for the Bucs is the division is still just as bad. Every NFC South team is 0-1.

20. Pittsburgh Steelers (1-0, LW: 20)

The Steelers got a win but it wasn't pretty. Facing a Falcons team down to its third quarterback, the Steelers led by just three points in the fourth quarter before T.J. Watt had an interception return for a touchdown. Particularly troubling was the offense, which had the worst success rate in the NFL for Week 1. The run game really struggled, with 2.8 yards per carry. And that's against a Falcons defense that wasn't projected to be very good.

19. Los Angeles Chargers (0-1, LW: 13)

There's nothing good to say about the Chargers' Week 1 loss. It was so dispiriting that head coach Jim Harbaugh lamented sitting his starters for most of the preseason. The offense, with new coordinator Mike McDaniel, had two plays longer than 15 yards against an Arizona defense that isn't expected to be good. (Don't tell Andrew Wingard I said that.) The defense, without last year's star coordinator Jesse Minter, allowed points or a missed field goal on seven of 10 possessions before a kneel-down at the end. The Chargers' early-season schedule is brutal, and the Cardinals game was supposed to be a rare easy win.

18. Green Bay Packers (0-1, LW: 17)

Nobody in Wisconsin wants to hear about how many yards Green Bay had or that the Packers outplayed the Vikings for most of the game. They want to know why the Packers, who lost five straight games last season, including multiple blown second-half leads, keep failing late in games. The Packers were outscored 22-0 in the fourth quarter. There has to be better answers for why the Packers are collapsing late. "It'll be a topic of conversation for all you guys until we do it," Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said. "That's the bottom line."

17. Minnesota Vikings (1-0, LW: 18)

The Vikings won and that's a great way to start the season, but it's not like they played well. They were outgained 419-239. The Packers had 6.3 yards per play to just 3.9 for the Vikings. Minnesota won a game in which it lost Kyler Murray in the first quarter to a concussion, so squeezing out a victory is still a very good result but improvement needs to be made, and a lot of that will depend on Murray's status.

16. Dallas Cowboys (0-1, LW: 7)

No team had a better EPA on offense than the Giants in Week 1 — which means no team had a worse EPA on defense than the Cowboys. Maybe team owner Jerry Jones was right to be "nervous" before kickoff Sunday night. Maybe everyone was too quick to assume that the Dallas' exhaustive defensive issues from a season ago were fixed. Despite new personnel and a new coordinator, the same communication issues that led to blown coverages showed up again in the loss to New York. Cowboys executive vice president Stephen Jones took a measured view of the wreckage, telling 105.3 The Fan (via The Athletic's Jon Machota): "Felt really good and still do about our football team. We just probably had a little unrealistic expectations in terms of what we could do, especially on the defensive side of the ball with all the new faces and a brand new coordinator." Indeed, nobody should completely overreact to Week 1. But after a horrendous performance in the season opener, the Cowboys' defense now has to show evidence, starting Week 2 vs. the Commanders, it's any better than it was last season.

15. Denver Broncos (0-1, LW: 4)

A lot will be made of coordinator Davis Webb taking over play-calling from Sean Payton and the Broncos' offense looking terrible in his first game doing it. That's not all that was wrong with Denver. The defense was rock solid last season but was miserable Monday night against the Chiefs. There were numerous missed tackles as the Chiefs rushed for more than 200 yards. The Broncos were very unlikely to replicate a 14-win season, but there was good reason to believe they were still capable of winning the AFC West again. They'll have to play far better on both sides of the ball if they want to keep the division race competitive this season.

14. New York Giants (1-0, LW: 23)

No team had a better offensive EPA per play through Sunday's Week 1 games than the Giants. Not even the Bears, who scored 59 points. What stood out was the impact new tight end Isaiah Likely had. He led the Giants with eight catches for 78 yards and two touchdowns. If the Giants' offense stays mostly healthy, perhaps this can be a surprise playoff team.

13. Houston Texans (0-1, LW: 10)

The defense should be fine when it's not facing Josh Allen. If that's the case, the positive about the loss to the Bills is that the offense looked good. Houston ranked ninth in offensive success rate through Sunday's games behind an improved rushing attack with David Montgomery and quarterback C.J. Stroud playing better. Stroud had 274 yards and two touchdowns with no interceptions. If that carries over, Houston is going to be good this season.

12. Cincinnati Bengals (1-0, LW: 15)

The Bengals' defense looked better. The Bucs' offense scored just 20 points and had fewer than 300 yards. Turnovers aren't guaranteed to carry over week to week but the Bengals forced four, including one that was returned for a touchdown. Cincinnati isn't going to be great on defense, but there have been some good teams to live off having a great offense and a defense that takes chances and makes a few game-changing plays. Maybe the Bengals can be that type of defense. That would be enough.

11. New England Patriots (0-1, LW: 5)

The overreaction directed at Drake Maye proves that the hate of the Patriots hasn't died just because Bill Belichick and Tom Brady are long gone. Maye didn't play well in the opener and didn't have a good postseason either. He played elite defenses in almost every game though. Maye is going to be good. He's just not able to overcome a middling supporting cast — A.J. Brown was out for the second half and TreVeyon Henderson was inactive in the opener — against great defenses as a third-year player. He's not nearly as bad as you'll read on social media.

10. Chicago Bears (1-0, LW: 11)

The Bears are going to be fun to watch. The offense was fantastic against a Panthers defense that isn't great but not that bad (22nd in defensive DVOA last season). They put up 59 points, a franchise record for a season opener, and 552 yards. That's great. They also allowed 37 points and 478 yards against a Panthers offense that was 25th in DVOA last season. Every game might be a pinball machine. And the Bears' offense might be so good it doesn't matter how much the defense allows. It's why they're not higher in the top 10.

9. Detroit Lions (1-0, LW: 9)

The Lions almost blew a 21-0 lead. They held on when they forced an incompletion on a 2-point conversion in overtime. Detroit's defense had played very well in building that lead, then let the Saints back in the game. Lions head coach Dan Campbell blamed the offense's inefficiency for the lead slipping away. "I'm like, man, we've got to be more efficient on offense," Campbell said. "We kind of spit and sputtered there and then they … had some tempo going."

The Lions face a very tough Week 2 game against the Bills, who will host their first regular-season game in their new stadium Thursday night.

8. Philadelphia Eagles (1-0, LW: 8)

The first look at new coordinator Sean Mannion's scheme wasn't great. Only the Steelers' offense had a lower success rate than the Eagles through Sunday's games. Jalen Hurts made some big plays, many of which were him creating something when nothing was open, and that saved the win. There's a long way to go for the offense.

7. Kansas City Chiefs (LW: 12)

Kenneth Walker III was excellent and will transform the Chiefs' offense. He had 173 yards rushing. Patrick Mahomes will be better as he get further removed from a torn ACL. He had just 184 yards passing and was off on many throws, but that didn't take away from a successful return. But one of the best stories of the opener was left tackle Kahlil Benson. He is an undrafted rookie out of Indiana who got no guaranteed money to sign with the Chiefs and did not play left tackle in college. He was forced into the lineup due to a Josh Simmons injury and there was rightful concern over him protecting Mahomes' blindside. But Benson, the first undrafted rookie to start Week 1 on the offensive line since Terence Steele with the Cowboys in 2020, played well and the Broncos rarely got any pressure on Mahomes. Offensive linemen don't get too much attention, but Benson deserves a lot of credit for stepping up when he had to.

6. Jacksonville Jaguars (1-0, LW: 14)

The Jaguars were fantastic last season. There was nothing fluky about their season. Then they looked dominant in Week 1. They led 31-0 early in the third quarter and if they wanted to run it up, the final score could have been really ugly for Cleveland. Jacksonville was one of two teams in the NFL in the top six of EPA per play and EPA allowed per play through Sunday's Week 1 games (Baltimore was the other). The Jaguars deserve respect.

5. San Francisco 49ers (1-0, LW: 16)

Few teams looked better than the 49ers in Week 1. It remains to be seen how the 49ers react to coming back from Australia, but their next two games are at home against the Dolphins and Cardinals. That helps. It's hard to buy that the 49ers can stay healthy — exciting rookie De'Zhaun Stribling suffered an ankle injury that will keep him out at least a month — but if they can then San Francisco showed it can be as good as anyone.

4. Los Angeles Rams (0-1, LW: 1)

We can't throw out everything we know because of one game. Maybe the Rams will be a huge disappointment this season, but it's too early to proclaim that. The Rams were the second-best team in the NFL last season and had a good offseason even before the Myles Garrett trade. Throughout the rankings, you'll see some teams that didn't move very much due to a great or bad Week 1. It's a one-game sample size for now.

3. Baltimore Ravens (1-0, LW: 6)

Had it not been for the Bears, we'd be talking more about how good the Ravens' offense looked. They gained 502 yards, and that was with a conservative second-half approach after losing receivers Zay Flowers and Ja'Kobi Lane to injuries. New offensive coordinator Declan Doyle was Ben Johnson's coordinator last season and the Ravens seem to have made a great hire with him. Keeping Lamar Jackson healthy is important, and the early receiver injuries are concerning, but the Ravens looked like a Super Bowl contender in Week 1.

2. Seattle Seahawks (1-0, LW: 2)

More disrespect for the Seahawks to not be No. 1. Your anger is understandable, Seattle fans. But the Sam Darnold injury sets the Seahawks back a bit until he returns. But there's no question about Seattle's defense, which was excellent against the Patriots and carried the team to a win. Maybe that's enough to carry the team as long as Drew Lock is at quarterback.

1. Buffalo Bills (1-0, LW: 3)

Had Bills-Texans happened in prime time, as it should have, we'd be even more excited about what Josh Allen did against a very good Houston defense. The 36 points the Bills put up was the most against Houston since 2023, which was DeMeco Ryans' first season as head coach. Allen threw for 334 yards and two touchdowns and rushed for 23 yards and two touchdowns. That win was a statement. The fact that it happened in the 1 p.m. Eastern window just means the Bills won't get as much hype as they should. That might change Thursday night when they face the Lions.

item.title: Brandon Cisse makes a good first impression
item.description: Cisse got beat, but got back up and kept competing.
item.content:encoded:
Nobody really wants to hear about bright spots after the way the Packers started the season, but there were a few in Week 1, and rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse was one of them.

Yes, Justin Jefferson got the better of him on one noteworthy play, but Justin Jefferson has a way of doing that. He’s victimized better corners than Cisse well past the first game of their career. But outside of Jefferson’s score, Cisse was on target and on task, playing 49 snaps in his first game in the NFL, the most of any Packers defender that didn’t hit 100% in Week 1.

The Packers’ defensive backfield has been the target of no small number of questions this offseason, but if this is what we can expect from Cisse, those questions should largely go away. He and Keisean Nixon will have their problems, I’m sure, but every competent snap helps every other defensive back do his job better.

That’s the real takeaway from Cisse’s performance. Rising tides in the secondary tend to carry all boats, and every decent performer takes just that much pressure off of everyone else. If Cisse continues to grow and perform well, it’ll only help a Packers team that can use all the help it can get right now.

item.title: Charvarius Ward embraces Guardian Cap in hopes of avoiding another concussion
item.description: After the 2025 season, Colts cornerback Charvarius Ward said that, if he gets another concussion, he'll "probably retire."
item.content:encoded:
After the 2025 season, Colts cornerback Charvarius Ward said that, if he gets another concussion, he'll "probably retire." To avoid that, he decided to try a Guardian Cap during the Week 1 game against the Ravens.

"I was scared to get knocked out again for real," Ward said earlier this week, via James Boyd of The Athletic. "So I just put a Guardian Cap on. I warmed up with it, and it felt good . . . I just kept it on all game. So I might as well keep it for the season. It's not gonna hurt me."

The real question is whether it helps.

"I don’t know if it made a difference or not," Ward said. "I got a headache right now. I don't think it's a concussion, but it is what it is. It's football, man. You're gonna get dinged up . . . I know what I signed up for."

The full benefits of the Guardian Cap aren't known. It helps with low-impact hits to the helmet. For bigger blows, will it make a difference?

One thing no helmet can do is prevent the brain from bouncing against the skull when the head quickly decelerates. Which is one way to get a concussion.

The NFL has a somewhat complicated relationship with the Guardian Cap. When the device was first adopted for use in practice, the league prevented players from wearing them during games. That position has changed; there are now one or two players in most games who can be seen wearing one.

The league is keenly aware of the aesthetics of the Guardian Cap. They're bulky. They diminish the appearance of the helmet. Even the new model, which doesn't require a cover for placement of logos and stripes, doesn't look the same as the helmet.

As helmets improve, the argument is that they are as effective as prior technology plus a Guardian Cap. But, still, the Guardian Cap will always provide an additional layer of cushioning.

And it's impossible to tell a player who wants to wear one that he can't do it. Even if it doesn't help that much. Even if it can create a false sense of security. Even if it doesn't look great on TV. At this point, if it helps a player like Ward break the tie between continuing his career and not playing, it needs to be among the available pieces of protective equipment for a game that is inherently hazardous to the human brain.

item.title: Falcons Week 1 3 up and 3 down: Defense is up, Offense is down
item.description: Who thrived and who stumbled against the Steelers?
item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Falcons couldn’t bring home the win in the season opener, but it wasn’t due to the defensive performances we saw. Unfortunately, the offense and special teams unit let the team down, a story many fans are tired of hearing.

Here’s the Week 1, 3 up and 3 down:

3 up

Sydney Brown

Acquiring Brown was one of Ian Cunningham’s first moves as GM, and it’s already shaping up to be one of his best. When Brown signed, the initial thought was that he’d be a good special teams contributor and competent depth, but Jeff Ulbrich had bigger plans.

Brown was more than depth in the season opener; he was essentially a starter, logging 30 snaps and making every one count. Brown was a force in the box, blowing up runs without fear and getting ball carriers on the ground almost immediately. He also blew up the screen play that led to a fumble recovery. It’s going to be fun to see how his role evolves on this defense, because he’s making it tough to keep him off the field.

Za’Darius Smith

Expectations were low for Smith entering Week 1; he was ready to call it a career and joined the team late. Smith blew those expectations out of the water. On just 16 snaps, he logged 2 sacks, providing the defense with the finisher they desperately needed after losing both Jalon Walker and James Pearce Jr.

Smith’s role is expected to grow as the season progresses, but getting production out of him this early on a limited snap count is hopefully a sign of even better things to come for the veteran.

Maason Smith

Smith was acquired in a player-for-player trade involving Ruke Orhorhoro. The initial take was that this was a lemon swap between two franchises disappointed with their 2nd-round investments. One man’s trash is another man’s treasure.

Smith was a force early, splitting double teams and pushing the pocket. If not for a questionable penalty, he would’ve finished the afternoon with a sack. Atlanta has needed a physical presence in the middle of their front, and while it’s too early to say the problem is officially solved, this performance brings the team one step closer to checking that box.

3 down

Matthew Bergeron

It was a middling effort for the Falcons offensive line overall, but when you’re the highest-paid member, the spotlight will always be on you. Many questioned the price tag attached to Bergeron’s extension, and those questions still linger after this week’s performance.

The left guard committed two holding penalties after getting beat clean off the snap. He also blew an assignment when pulling to the backside of the run, resulting in a negative play. There were flashes of good play but not enough to justify the new deal. Jake Matthews and Chris Lindstrom also had off days, so the hope is this was just the group still adjusting to the new scheme.

Nick Folk

The most accurate kicker from 2025 doubled his miss count in the 2026 opener. The 54-yard miss is somewhat understandable; at his age, that could be just outside of his range. However, the 45-yard miss was inexcusable. Yes, Pittsburgh is a notoriously difficult place to kick, but when the team signed Folk, it was with the expectation that he would be able to overcome those difficult environments.

We aren’t hitting the panic button yet; Folk finished 2/4 on the day, but fans will be feeling a little less confident when he steps on the field for the next few games.

Cooper Rush

Rush was thrust into the starting role after Tua Tagovailoa was downgraded with an oblique strain. Rush then started experiencing back spasms the day before the game, and looked uncomfortable from the first snap. It was clear that the ball wasn’t getting aired out in this matchup, and even completing simple screens became a monumental task.

It was interesting to see he had success on the few play-action concepts run Sunday, and if he’s starting again in Week 2, Rees needs to lean into those concepts more if he wants to salvage the passing game.

While the Falcons didn’t get the win, all hope isn’t lost. This defense has legitimate pieces that will keep the Falcons in games all season. If the offense and special teams can pull their weight, this team can win games this year. The team will host the Carolina Panthers in Week 2, who’ve had the Falcons number lately.

item.title: Eagles restructure Nolan Smith's contract
item.description: The Eagles have created some cap space for this season and next season.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles have created some cap space for this season and next season.

The team has restructured the contract of linebacker Nolan Smith. Spotrac reports that converting $1.24 million of his 2026 salary created $992,000 in cap space for the rest of this season.

Smith also had $12.5 million of his salary for 2027 — the Eagles exercised their fifth-year option on his rookie deal — converted to a bonus. That move opened up $10 million in cap space for next season.

The Eagles may or may not have their eye on making an immediate addition to the roster, but the restructuring gives the that option and the extra cap space in 2027 can help General Manager Howie Roseman structure things in a way that keeps the Eagles in compliance with the cap now and in the future.

item.title: Titans must start Cedric Gray, Anthony Hill at LB in Week 2
item.description: The Tennessee TItans need to start Cedric Gray and Anthony Hill Jr. at linebacker in Week 2 versus the Eagles.
item.content:encoded:
The only positive takeaway from the Tennessee Titans’ Week 1 blunder was the performance of rookie linebacker Anthony Hill Jr. The 60th overall selection in the 2026 NFL Draft recorded a team-high 16 tackles. The Titans need to start Hill and Cedric Gray at linebacker versus the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 2.

Hill started in place of Gray, who failed to clear concussion protocol in time for Week 1 after suffering an off-field leisure accident. That put Hill in the starting lineup next to veteran Cody Barton. The rookie took full advantage of the opportunity.

Head coach Robert Saleh confirmed that Gray has already cleared protocol during his Monday press conference. That opens up the possibility for the Titans to start Gray and Hill in Week 2. They must be bold enough to send Barton to the bench, especially versus an athletic Eagles offense.

Hill didn’t just register 16 tackles. He appeared to have forced and recovered a fumble in Jets territory when he punched the ball loose from sophomore tight end Mason Taylor. The refs called an incomplete pass on the field, and surprisingly upheld that call once Saleh challenged it.

Even with his takeaway confusingly stolen from him, Hill still made impact plays. The former Texas standout had a really nice pass breakup on a peanut-punch, breaking up a pass for a Jets running back on a wheel route. Hill also shoved Geno Smith out of bounds short of the sticks on a third-and-short, forcing a fourth down.

The rebuilding Titans are still stacking young talent. They aggressively traded up for Hill, nabbing him with a second-round pick they initially didn’t have. That decision paid immediate dividends in Week 1. The Titans were terrible, but Hill was excellent. Hopefully he starts opposite Gray versus the Eagles in Week 2.

item.title: Bills and Texans each fumbled twice, Bills recovered all four on way to 36-31 win
item.description: Bills coach Joe Brady cited the importance of O'Cyrus Torrence recovering James Cook's fumble on the game-winning drive.
item.content:encoded:
The Bills' 36-31 win over the Texans could have gone the other way if some fumbled footballs had bounced a little differently.

Both teams fumbled twice in the game, and the Bills recovered all four fumbles. In a one-possession game that was decided when the Bills recovered C.J. Stroud's second fumble with nine seconds left, any one of those fumbles landing in a Texan's hands could have altered the outcome. All four fumbles going the other way almost certainly would have given the Texans the win.

Another crucial fumble recovery came when Bills running back James Cook put the ball on the ground with three minutes left in the fourth quarter and the Bills trailing 31-30. If the Texans had recovered that, they might have been able to run out the clock and win the game. Instead, Bills offensive lineman O'Cyrus Torrence recovered the fumble and the Bills scored the game-winning touchdown later in that drive.

Bills head coach Joe Brady noted that the hustle of Torrence, whom the team calls Cyborg or Cybo, was crucial to the win.

"We put the ball on the ground there," Brady said. "If our offensive line isn't doing the little things we ask and run to the football, and Cybo doesn't recover that football, and we end up losing that game, a lot of people will point to the fact that we fumbled. And we did fumble. It can't be just because we won the football game that, 'Oh, that didn't happen, we had no turnovers.'"

Brady said Cook was mad at himself for fumbling and that the Bills aren't overlooking how fortunate they were on fumble recoveries.

"He was pissed. I talked to him on the plane. He knows how important he is to our football team," Brady said of Cook. "He understands that when he has the ball he has all of our jobs on the line. He was not happy after that. Even through the win, we've got to clean that up."

Brady knows the Bills can't count on recovering 100 percent of fumbles every week.
