item.title: 2026 Minnesota Golden Gophers in the NFL: Week 1
item.description: It was a great week for some former Gophers, and a disappointing inactive week for several others
item.content:encoded:
Week One of the NFL season has come and gone and there were a few standout performances from former Gophers, and a few disappointing results. We are seeing a changing of the guard as some of the Gophers from the early 2020’s are seeing their roles be significantly diminished, but also some of the youngest Gophers in the NFL are struggling to see the field. It’s only Week one so way to early to see any trends, but it will be something to watch as the season rolls on. Below see how the ex-Gophers did in Week 1 and a look ahead to Week 2.

Arizona Cardinals

Week 1 @ Los Angeles Chargers
Week 2 vs Seattle Seahawks

Jack Gibbons-LB

Gibbons started at linebacker for Arizona and played 54 of 55 defensive snaps while adding another 11 on special teams. He played a large role in Arizona’s upset win over the Chargers finishing with a team high seven tackles, five of them solo, a half of a sack and a QB hit.

Baltimore Ravens

Week 1 @ Indianapolis Colts
Week 2 vs New Orleans Saints

Rashod Bateman-WR

Bateman will be an interesting player to watch this season as his role appears to be shrinking on the Ravens. He played 53 offensive snaps which was 78% but was only targeted once by Lamar Jackson and did not make the catch. With Zay Flowers suffering a hamstring injury, it will be interesting to see if Bateman is a larger target this week.

Cincinnati Bengals

Week 1 vs Tampa Bay Buccaneers
Week 2 @ Houston Texans

Boye Mafe—DE

Mafe had an amazing debut on the Bengals defensive line in their win over Tampa Bay. He played 37 defensive snaps or 65% and finished with just one solo tackle. But that tackle was a strip sack of Baker Mayfield in the fourth quarter. He also recovered a Bucky Irving fumble in the first quarter. Not a bad start in the orange and black. He will likely go against fellow former Gopher Aireontae Ersery this Sunday in what could be a fun battle.

Dallas Cowboys

Week 1 @ New York Giants—Sunday Night
Week 2 vs Washington Commanders

Brevin Span-Ford—TE

Span-Ford played 13 offensive snaps and another 11 on special teams in the loss to the Giants. He was targeted twice by Dak Prescott and made both catches for 14 yards. He also added a special teams tackle. Unfortunately he likely lost a bet to Prescott on the results of Saturday’s game between their two colleges.

Though he probably doesn’t care after he signed a new three year contract extention worth $18 million with $12.075 million guaranteed. Not too shabby for an undrafted tight end.

Green Bay Packers

Week 1 @ Minnesota Vikings
Week 2 @ New York Jets

Benjamin St. Juste—CB

St. Juste played mostly on special teams with 23 special teams snaps and just one defensive snap in the loss. He recorded one solo tackle.

Houston Texans

Week 1 vs Buffalo Bills
Week 2 vs Cincinnati Bengals

Aireontae Ersery—OT

Ersery played all 79 offensive snaps and five more on special teams in the close loss to Buffalo. He did pick up a false start penalty on the opening drive of the season.

Indianapolis Colts

Week 1 vs Baltimore Ravens
Week 2 @ Kansas City Chiefs—Sunday Night

Justin Walley—CB

Walley made his NFL debut and played 39 defensive snaps and another seven on special teams in the loss to the Ravens. He finished with six tackles, five of them solo.

Jacksonville Jaguars

Week 1 vs Cleveland Browns
Week 2 @ Denver Broncos

Eric Murray—S

Murray started and played jus 33 defensive snaps and seven special teams snaps sitting most of the fourth quarter of the blowout win over Cleveland. He recorded a pair of tackles, one of them solo.

Daniel Faalele—OG

Faalele was a healthy scratch for the game and was inactive.

Danny Striggow—DE

Striggow saw extra time in the blowout late and played 24 defensive snaps and five more on special teams. He recored two tackles, one of them solo.

Las Vegas Raiders

Week 1 vs Miami Dolphins
Week 2 @ Los Angeles Chargers

Cody Lindenberg—LB

Lindenberg was a surprise scratch for Sunday’s win over Miami as it appeared he had a backup linebacker spot locked up.

Minnesota Vikings

Week 1 vs Green Bay Packers
Week 2 @ Chicago Bears

Max Brosmer—QB-Practice Squad

Brosmer was not active for the game, but could potentially be the emergency third QB this week if Kyler Murray needs to miss the game with his concussion.

Blake Cashman—LB

Cashman was once again an absolute stud for the Vikings on defense. He played 65 defensive snapa and one more on special teams and finished with seven tackles, five of them solo, two for a loss, with two QB hits and a half of a sack of Jordan Love. Not too shabby.

New Orleans Saints

Week 1 @ Detroit Lions
Week 2 @ Baltimore Ravens

Jordan Howden—S

The Saints dropped a heartbreaker in OT to Detroit to open the season. Howden only saw special teams action playing 23 snaps and picking up a pair of tackles, one of which was solo.

New York Jets

Week 2 vs Green Bay Packers

Tyler Johnson—WR—Practice Squad

After being released by Dallas in training camp, Johnson was signed to the Jets practice squad this week. He played 12 games for the Jets a season ago so it’s very possible he could see a call up in the future.

New York Giants

JMS started and played all 69 starts at center for the Giants offense in their win.

Tyler Nubin—S

Nubin did regain his starting role and played all 58 defensive snaps and four more on special teams in the win. He ended with three solo tackles.

Pittsburgh Steelers

Neither player was called up for the game and both remained on the practice squad.

Week 2 @ Arizona Cardinals

Kallerup was a healthy scratch and was inactive for the season opening game.

item.title: The Good and the Bad from the Chiefs’ win over the Broncos
item.description: Staff analyst Nate Christensen sorts through the positives and negatives from Kansas City’s season-opening win.
item.content:encoded:
Football is back!

The Kansas City Chiefs beat the Denver Broncos 31-10 on “Monday Night Football” in dominant fashion, making it one of my favorite Chiefs wins in years.

The crowd and energy were fantastic, and the Chiefs bludgeoned Denver with physicality and power on both sides of the ball. It was an incredibly impressive performance that was very enjoyable to watch.

There’s a ton to analyze, so this season I’ll structure film reviews around two or three topics each week. In wins, I’ll cover two positives and one negative; in losses, we’ll point out two negatives and only one positive.

Let’s start with the positives.

The Good

Chiefs playing extra offensive linemen

I absolutely loved what the Chiefs did in the run game against the Broncos. It started from the very beginning. Head coach Andy Reid, notorious for his love of the passing game, came out on national television and sent a message to every NFL team: we’re going to run the ball.

Kenneth Walker will get most of the headlines for the improved run game, and rightfully so. You couldn’t have asked for a better debut. Walker showed big-play explosiveness, but also patience and vision between the tackles. His tackle-breaking was elite, and he showed power with his stiff arm and by running through defenders.

But that wasn’t my favorite part of the Chiefs’ run game. Four times in this game, Andy Reid checked in backup guard Hunter Nourzad and nose tackle Khyris Tonga on short-yardage plays; reserve lineman Josh Ezeudu also saw time.

Kansas City used the “Jumbo” packages to move the chains, and I loved the decision. Essentially, they had two options: extra offensive linemen or tight ends. They chose the linemen.

Normally, the trade-off is that extra linemen reduce the pass threat. Defenses don’t have to account for them in coverage, making the run more obvious and letting defenders attack downhill (although I would like to see a Khyris Tonga touchdown).

But with this Chiefs’ roster, the tight ends don’t provide enough of a passing threat to justify keeping them on the field. Teams aren’t worried about covering Noah Gray or Jared Wiley (a gameday inactive) downfield, while Travis Kelce is now limited to a smaller area of the field. The Chiefs simply don’t have enough receiving talent at tight end for defenses to adjust much anyway.

So why not just add another lineman and improve your run blocking?

There’s obviously a limit to how often you can use jumbo personnel, but I like that the Chiefs are willing to turn to it when needed.

An improved pressure plan

Broncos quarterback Bo Nix was pressured at the fourth-highest rate in the NFL this week at 45.5%. Last season, the Chiefs’ pressure rate was 34.4%, 15th in the NFL. More pressure was an offseason priority, and they delivered on Monday.

Multiple factors contributed. First, some of the young defensive linemen they brought in made an immediate impact. The most noticeable was defensive end R Mason Thomas, who finished with two pressures and a sack on 19 pass-rush snaps. Thomas didn’t get off to the best start, but found his rhythm as the game progressed. Thomas’ sack was particularly impressive, showing the lower-body flexibility to spin back inside after trying to get upfield.

Felix Anudike-Uzomah also impacted the game with a strip sack. Surprisingly, the Chiefs had FAU inside at defensive tackle during this game, despite his smaller frame. On his sack, he showed impressive power in a swim move to turn upfield.

But more than the defensive line, the Chiefs’ blitzes were outstanding. The team blitzed just 30.3% of the time, 14th in the NFL this week, but were incredibly effective when they did.

Early in the game, the Chiefs brought cornerback Nohl Williams on a blitz from a condensed formation as the Broncos looked for a big play. Williams got a sack and changed the tone of this game. From there, the Broncos mostly called short passes against the blitz, but the Chiefs were all over them, dropping defenders into hot zones and forcing Nix to hold onto the ball.

Another thing the Chiefs scouted was that they wanted to keep running back R.J. Harvey in pass protection. Harvey is not a big back and struggles in those situations, and the Chiefs picked on that all night. Linebacker Nick Bolton’s sack was a one-on-one with Harvey where he blows him up and then swims around him.

The speed of the new defensive linemen will help the four-man pass rush and the blitzes. One problem the Chiefs had last year was poor blitz spacing because their defensive linemen couldn’t get upfield to occupy blockers. Thomas now gives them that, alongside a guy who can win one-on-one. The Chiefs defense sent a message to the NFL that they’re going to hit the quarterback more this year.

The bad

The Chiefs’ passing game

Most of the game was outstanding for the Chiefs, but the pass game struggled. Mahomes was 7-for-17 passing at halftime for 56 yards. At one point, the Chiefs had six straight incompletions. Kansas City’s leading wide receiver in receiving yards was Rashee Rice with 19 yards. The Chiefs’ wide receivers had five total catches. Mahomes was 29th in average depth of target this week at 4.7 yards.

Frankly, the Chiefs got lucky on the two best passing plays of the game. Rashee Rice had two defenders in position to tackle him on his touchdown, and both whiffed badly. Tight end Travis Kelce’s catch and run was a great hot read to beat the blitz, but the amount of space he had was crazy and rarely happens in the NFL.

Outside of those two plays, the Chiefs’ passing game was inept. The group struggled with quick-game concepts because the Broncos were sitting on every underneath route. At one point, Kansas City ran back-to-back screens to Walker, and Denver blew both up.

The Broncos dared the Chiefs to throw downfield, and they couldn’t. Nobody could separate against Denver’s cornerbacks. Rice had virtually no impact outside of his touchdown. Xavier Worthy saw six targets but caught just three for 18 yards, while wide receivers Tyquan Thornton and Cyrus Allen didn’t record a catch.

The Chiefs will face less talented secondaries moving forward, and getting left tackle Josh Simmons back should give the quarterback more time for receivers to get open.

But the reality is the Chiefs don’t have enough pass-catching talent right now. Teams aren’t threatened by their receivers, and they don’t have a player who can consistently beat man coverage. Until that changes, the passing game has a limited ceiling. I don’t think the answer is on the roster, so the Chiefs may have to look outside the organization at the trade deadline for someone who can provide that missing juice.

item.title: Broncos at Chiefs: The No Bull Review
item.description: No Bull thoughts, opinions, and analysis on the Denver Broncos being blown out by the Kansas City Chiefs
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos decided to run it back with the best continuity in the NFL, brought in a top-tier wide receiver free agent, and had a healthy Bo Nix for week 1 of the NFL season. What did we get for all the chatter about being a Super Bowl ready team?  An absolute butt stain of a performance from the Broncos on offense and defense.

31 – 10 is an embarrassment. Some may take great joy at digging into the failures and faults at every orifice of an abomination of a game, but I honestly find less and less joy doing that the more years I add to my belt. I’ve got some points to make worth talking about, but largely we’ll use the review to talk big picture (kinda my normal routine in recent years when the Broncos lay an absolute egg).

Head Coach

Sean Payton, for some strange reason, doesn’t understand how to get his teams ready to hit the gates running. He runs a complex offense that is scheme-dependent (which I honestly love because it works well when executed properly).

He doesn’t seem to value playing starters much in the preseason, with many vets getting a couple of series in the warm-up games. It is hard to analyze this performance and not cast some doubt on the process being used when his teams year after year have problems executing early in the season.

This team on both sides of the ball looked very unprepared for this game. The offense had no clue how to find a groove and keep it or how to execute any 3rd down play effectively. The “best offensive line in the NFL” pass blocked like a car full of clowns at a diarrhea fiesta. The defense looked like a unit full of undrafted rookies trying to make a big turnover on every play and forgetting that this is the kind of football where they have to tackle.

Payton often takes the fault immediately in his pressers when the team plays this poorly, and I’m sure he did this week as well. Yes, Payton. It indeed is your fault. You did not prepare your team properly to play this game. You were outcoached in the most predictable ways. 

I’m a friggin nobody fan chugging Mountain Dews and eating Cheetos, and I knew the Kansas City Chiefs were going to run multiple tight ends / extra offensive linemen like the Bills did last year and run the ball with Kenneth Walker on repeat as their one and only way to create offensive production. Your team had no plan for that.

Bo Nix’s one biggest weakness is his reluctance to throw the ball over the middle, and yet another offseason went by without any evidence of work being done to address that weakness. It kinda makes it easy to defend the pass when your QB only uses ⅔ of the field the majority of the time.

Offense

So let’s just say that all the talk about how awesome Davis Webb is and how ready he is for the play-calling duties is looking quite sus at this point in time. That looked like a weaker version of the offense we saw last year, with a play caller abandoning the run when it didn’t need to be, getting fancy on 3rd and short when you could have just run the friggin ball for an easy first down, and leaning on underneath throws when you just traded for one of the most potent downfield threats in the NFL.

I do know that not all the calls were terrible. I liked a lot of the plays that they threw to Pat Bryant. I thought Waddle and Sutton both dropped catchable balls. I thought Nix lost plays quite often by trying to go outside instead of simply stepping up and throwing the ball. The execution on offense was lacking from the player side of things.

Also, why are we still having to use timeouts and getting delays of game when we have this nifty young play caller? I thought this move was put in place to address that?

One small pass I give the offense and Bo Nix that is worth mentioning is the wind. In the 2nd and 4th quarters, when the offense played its worst was when the wind was in their face, which is going to make most QBs more timid about throwing over the middle or deeper down the field. Those would have been great quarters to lean on the run game in my mind, but hey…the game plan called for check downs and screens…right?

Quarterbacks

Bo Nix looked like a rookie, plain and simple. The moment of this game was far too big for him. His early interception was horrendous, unforgivable, and pathetic. He stared down the only option on that side of the field, watched a guy with perfect technique defend it. Then Bo decided to throw him the ball (because there was a 0% chance of our guy ever catching that ball).

The happy feet are back big time. The line did him no favors (regardless of how much Payton wants to crow about sacks being a quarterback stat). If Bo was audibling out of runs or choosing the pass option in RPOs, he needs coaching because we have backs who can run effectively now.

Line

Mike McGlinchey had an awful night and owes the offense a dinner or two. He got worked multiple times and was a core piece of many pressures on the night.

Running Backs

I’d love to crow about our running backs. JK Dobbins averaged 4.5 ypc, and RJ Harvey averaged 6 (small sample size). It seems like we maybe could have done better than 30% of the plays on the night being runs if we wanted to. Before anyone says a word about the game going sideways, please note that the team had 17 passing attempts vs. 6 runs in the first half, with the game being within one score. Don’t take that excuse from Sean Payton, other fans, or silly announcers.

Receivers

The good news is that the team seems to have figured out how to make Evan Engram a part of the offense. Also, Pat Bryant is currently the best wide receiver on the team, and it isn’t close.

Cortland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle seemed to be largely placeholders on the field that Nix wasn’t interested in throwing to when coming open (which they were through the night constantly).

Oh yeah, and Troy Franklin still sucks. Let’s rotate Lil’Jordan Humphrey back in and let the potato get picked off the waiver wire.

Defense

We need to stop all talk about Vance Joseph being one of the best defensive coordinators in the NFL right this second. He can’t even get his team ready to stop a team that can only run their bell-cow back on repeat to gain yards. 

Heck, the team outside of Zach Allen and Patrick Surtain doesn’t even understand the fundamental process of how to tackle in the NFL at any level.

The effort of this defense was absolutely pathetic. The execution of this defense was what I would expect from a team of Pop Warner youths doped out on barbiturates.

Positive notes for the defense: Kansas City was holding on damn near every pass play, and it was insulting to the game of NFL football that they were allowed to get away with it…I had not seen this level of holding abuse since 2015. If you are worried about our pass rush, don’t be. They still have it, but the refs decided Kermit gets different rules than other more common quarterbacks in the NFL.

Front 7

The continued story of Alex Singleton being a liability at inside linebacker is alive and well. He was an embarrassment at linebacker with 2 good tackles out of his 15 in the game (let me point out again that getting a lot of tackles does not equate to a linebacker being good…where they make the tackle is rather important). We extended the worst starter on the team. I’m glad he’s a team captain and a feel-good story. I have never felt good about his play over any three-game stretch of his time here and have quite regularly thought he was a liability and a minus player for this defense.

Secondary

I had notes on many defensive backs in this game with good plays, but sadly had just as many of the same players missing a tackle. I’m not giving your name time when you can’t even square a player and wrap up properly on an NFL field. Hit the tackle dummies, boys…you need the work.

Special Teams

Jeremy Crawshaw has a phenomenal leg. He was the most effective player on the whole roster on Monday Night. Now pardon me while I go puke after typing that.

Final Thoughts

Now that we’ve exercised the demons of this game, let me say that this was just one game. It is cliché, but true. This game sucked. The team is 0-1. We have 16 games left in the season. There’s a lot of football to be played.

This team is capable of so much more than they showed in Week 1 in every way. The season is far from over. Losing to the Chiefs stings, but it is only actually bad if they somehow sustain wins and we lose to them at home.

This team spent all last season believing in each other and fighting hard every week to get better. Maybe they just need a bigger chip on their shoulder in order to get locked in and play how we know they are capable of playing.

I will say this schedule does NOT get easier. The Chiefs were one of the weaker teams we were facing in the first 6 weeks (Mahomes sucked and still isn’t throwing well). Buckle up, Broncos Country. We may have a bumpy ride in the next few weeks.

The New Orleans Saints will hit the road in Week 2 to take on the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium this Sunday.

These two teams first met on September 29, 1996, in the Louisiana Superdome, with Baltimore coming away with a 17-10 victory. Since then, they have played one another just eight times, with the Ravens holding a 6-2 advantage in the all-time series.

The last time they faced one another, Baltimore defeated New Orleans 27-13 in the Caesars Superdome on November 7, 2022. The Ravens controlled much of the game, with Lamar Jackson and Baltimore’s rushing attack proving difficult for the Saints to contain.

New Orleans did not earn its first victory over Baltimore until 2018, when the Saints escaped M&T Bank Stadium with a thrilling 24-23 win that ended when then Ravens kicker Justin Tucker missed an extra point with 24 seconds remaining.

The Saints enter Sunday’s matchup looking to bounce back after a heartbreaking 31-30 overtime loss to the Detroit Lions in Week 1. New Orleans fell behind 21-0 before mounting an impressive comeback, eventually forcing overtime and having multiple opportunities to get the upset.

Despite three turnovers, quarterback Tyler Shough threw for 410 yards and three touchdowns, while Chris Olave finished with 10 receptions for 182 yards. The performance offered plenty of reasons for optimism despite the loss, especially after the Saints showed the resilience to battle back from a three-touchdown deficit on the road.

Baltimore enters the matchup 1-0 after opening its season with a 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts. The Ravens piled up 506 yards of total offense, led by Lamar Jackson’s 324 passing yards and Derrick Henry’s 144 rushing yards and three touchdowns.

For the Saints, Sunday’s matchup represents another difficult early-season road test and an opportunity to build on the fight they showed in Detroit. Baltimore has historically had the upper hand in this series, but New Orleans will look to change that while earning its first victory of the 2026 season.

item.title: Cowboys defense is still the problem after loss to Giants
item.description: It is so frustrating how big of a problem the defense remains.
item.content:encoded:
Football is back, and for Dallas Cowboys fans around the world, so is the disappointment that is often associated with this team. For the better part of 60 minutes, the Dallas Cowboys were taken to task by their division rival, the Giants. Both sides of the ball struggled, leading to a season-opening loss, but today we are going to talk about… that’s right, the defense.

This defense still has a long way to go

The play above can sum up the sputtering start to what was supposed to be a vastly improved defensive unit in 2026. Over the offseason, the Cowboys spent a lot of draft capital trying to revamp what was statistically the worst defense in franchise history last season. Dallas even hired a new defensive coordinator, Christian Parker, and many fans and pundits alike believed that this defense would not, could not, reach the levels of profound doom that this unit sank to last year.

People expected Vic Fangio; instead, they got Eberflus 2.0, and the Giants essentially did whatever they wanted, limiting the Cowboys to two offensive possessions in the entire second half. By the third quarter, players were already worn out; their effort was questionable, and they couldn’t stop the Giants’ offense.

The defensive line was bad. They sacked Dart twice, but one of them came from Caleb Downs on a blitz. The Cowboys rank 21st in Week 1 pressure rate despite blitzing at the seventh-highest rate. The ends constantly failed to set the edge, got lost in coverage and were completely ineffective at rushing the passer.

The linebackers may have been worse. Winters had a horrible game, rating in the 40s by PFF; he was consistently lost in coverage and did little to make up for it. Overshown got hurt again, but did little to move the needle when he was in. Barham pulled up, inexplicably, on the Giants’ last touchdown that you saw earlier, after they spammed a checkdown four straight times.

The secondary was okay, only to be diced up by Dart when they needed stops on third down the most. They were close but never in good positions to make plays; Dart made them pay as the Giants converted a nearly record-high clip of third downs (9/11). What’s more concerning is that new Dallas Cowboys DC Christian Parker is supposed to be a secondary guru. His nickel package had the second-most snaps and gave up eight yards per play.

What’s the bright side

The bright side is, it’s week one. Caleb Downs looked solid; he gave up seven yards on two receptions when targeted, led the team in sacks with one, forced a fumble and, at times, seemed to be the only player on the defense interested in playing.

The alarm bells don’t necessarily need to be sounding yet, but there are very scary signs that this defense may not have gotten any better. The regular season isn’t the time to make major adjustments; it is the time to show what you’ve done in the offseason. If week one is any indication, these mental lapses and poor play are bad habits carried over from last year. It will once again be a very long year in Big D unless Parker can make some quick fixes.

item.content:encoded:
The Commanders are adding a veteran offensive lineman to the roster ahead of their Week 2 game in Dallas.

According to multiple reports, they are signing Lucas Patrick. Patrick was in camp with the Giants and missed time with a knee injury before being released at the end of the summer.

Patrick played in six games for the Bengals in 2025 and appeared in 107 games for the Packers, Bears and Saints earlier in his career. He has made 65 career starts while seeing time at guard and center.

The Commanders add experienced depth with the move. Nick Allegretti started at center in Week 1 with Chris Paul and Sam Cosmi next to him at the guard spots.

item.title: Commanders free agency: Washington reportedly signing veteran center/guard
item.description: The Commanders add desperately needed interior O-line help with the reported signing of center/guard Lucas Patrick
item.content:encoded:
The Commanders are reportedly signing veteran interior offensive lineman Lucas Patrick, who has extensive experience playing center and both guard spots.  

The Ringer’s Tom Peliserro was first to report the news on Wednesday morning.  

Patrick came to Washington’s training complex on Tuesday for a visit and the side ended up agreeing on a pact.  

Patrick has 65 starts in 113 professional games, with time spent in Green Bay, Chicago, New Orleans and Cincinnati leading into this year. He spent training camp with the New York Giants, where he dealt with knee issues and lost the backup center job. He was cut when rosters were trimmed to 53.  

The knee injury might’ve necessitated the facility visit, allowing it to be examined before signing. As a matter of process, Patrick’s base salary is not guaranteed after signing post-Week 1.

The addition’s corresponding move will be known later on Wednesday.

The Commanders have struggled to find interior depth, especially at the center spot. Nick Allgretti missed significant time this summer with a calf strain, and Julian Good-Jones (now on the practice squad) and rookie Matt Gulbin clearly weren’t ready to assume starter’s duties.  

Patrick is an established pro, but we’ll have to see how he fits and what he’s able to contribute once he works into the Commanders culture and position group. Odds seem great that he’ll be the top reserve at center and both guard spots when he can get up to speed.

The Commanders’ Dilemma: Protect Jayden Daniels or Let Him Loose?

In Week 1, Washington’s young quarterback stuck to a new script until his team needed a hero

In a perfect world, the Commanders wouldn’t have to choose between keeping their franchise quarterback healthy and winning games. In a perfect world — such as the one they inhabited in 2024, when Daniels was a spectacular rookie and the Commanders were a 12-5 juggernaut — they can accomplish both objectives.

But here, at the start of the 2026 season, it’s already feeling like something close to a binary choice. And for most of Sunday night’s entertaining game, it felt like the Commanders were unsure which side of that line they wanted to occupy.

For the first three quarters Sunday night, the Commanders mostly stuck to that script. And what did that get them? A 17-9 deficit. Nine completions in 24 attempts for Daniels, for a total of 65 passing yards. No sacks, but no touchdown passes. Their longest play from scrimmage at that point was for 15 yards. They were 2 for 11 on third-down conversions. Terry McLaurin, their two-time Pro Bowl wideout, had two targets and no catches.

They absolutely, positively, 100% don’t want Daniels to feel like he has to go out there and win games for them with his unique blend of athleticism, artistry and aerial acumen. Until they absolutely, positively, 100% need him to do exactly that. And then, it seems, they are willing to hold their breath and turn him loose.

Joshua Josephs keeps turning limited Commanders chances into lasting impressions

Just how much time Josephs will see on the field now that edge rusher Dorance Armstrong Jr. is back from his one-game suspension remains to be seen. But if the No. 147 overall selection in the 2026 NFL Draft keeps making this kind of impact against elite-level tackles like Johnson, it’ll stay on the radar.

At the very least.

These Week 1 flashes weren’t without substance, either.

Josephs was among the standout performers at training camp, displaying the speed, length, and dynamism that convinced the Commanders to take a chance. He backed this up in the preseason, even scoring a touchdown by bursting onto a loose football against the Detroit Lions.

His stunning special teams effort went viral. To Tyler Owens, it was ‘just a normal football play’

It wasn’t the first time Tyler Owens ripped down the field to slam a returner to the ground. It wasn’t even the first time in that game.

But in the second quarter of the Washington Commanders’ loss to the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday, Owens’ play as a special-teams gunner made him a household name literally overnight.

Facing a vise, or double-team, in punt coverage, Owens split Eagles jammers Jonathan Jones (a former Commander) and Darius Cooper by essentially tossing them to the side and leaving them in his wake as he pursued returner Britain Covey — whom he then lifted off the ground and body-slammed at Philadelphia’s 38-yard line.

“I feel like it was just a normal football play out there,” Owens told The Athletic on Tuesday.

Commanders Film Review: Sonny Styles vs Eagles

One of the main reasons Styles was drafted so highly was due to his athleticism. He is the definition of an athletic freak and while he adjusts to the mental side of the game at the NFL level, his athleticism can carry him through to be productive. Against the Eagles on Sunday, we saw that athleticism stand out in a number of different situations.

As soon as the ball is snapped, Styles triggers and gets a full head of steam as he works up to Barkley. Barkley has to abandon the play-action fake because Styles covers the ground so quickly. He attempts to get low and get under Styles in order to redirect his momentum upwards and stall out the rush, but Styles runs over him.

Barkley is one of the premier running backs in this league. He’s listed at 6-foot, 233 pounds, which is big for a running back. He’s been one of the hardest backs to tackle and bring down in the NFL since he was drafted. This is not someone who just gets run over by a better athlete. Typically Barkley is the one running over people as the better athlete. But Styles gets low, gets his hands on Barkley’s chest and uses his momentum to knock Barkley off his feet and run through the block. Styles then quickly turns his attention to Jalen Hurts, who is another player that is very hard to bring down.

But even when he wasn’t making freaky plays against Barkley, the athleticism still stood out.

How did the Giants’ 2026 rookie class play against the Dallas Cowboys?

Arvell Reese

The fifth overall pick was on the field for 62 total plays, including 11 penalties, two Cowboys’ kickoffs, and the Giants’ lone punt.

Reese was, overall, as advertised. He’s a big, long, and highly athletic linebacker who looked the part surrounded by the Giants’ other big, long, and athletic linebackers. He also showed off his football IQ all game long. Reese is a highly active communicator in the pre-snap phase, and he also appears to process quickly after the ball is snapped. He wastes little time getting to his landmarks, picking up pass catchers in coverage, or coming downhill to play the run. He also clearly understands where his gap responsibilities are, as well as where the defense is trying to funnel the ball.

Reese looks smooth and rangy dropping into coverage at the second level, easily getting depth and into his coverage zones. He also did a good job of using his hands to keep blockers from latching on to him and allowing him to navigate traffic in pursuit. We also got to see Reese’s strength and violence as a tackler when the time came to get the ball carrier on the ground.

Reese wasn’t quite as flashy as former teammates Sonny Styles and Caleb Downs, but he did finish second to Tremaine Edmunds in total tackles. I’d like to see more splash plays from Reese, and I think we will as the season progresses, but this was an impressive introduction for the linebacker.

item.title: ‘Hungry and humble’ FB Patrick Ricard embodies the John Harbaugh Giants
item.description: “I want to impose my will on defenses.”
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants talked … and talked … and talked as the season approached about being a physical football team. Even as the Giants were building the foundation of their offense, “we know it will be physical” was the answer you would get when asking what it might look like.

We saw the physicality the Giants want to bring to the table during Sunday’s 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys, with Dallas COO Stephen Jones even admitting “they outphysicaled us.”

The poster child for that physicality, and for the kind of football team head coach John Harbaugh wants the Giants to be, is 300-pound fullback Patrick Ricard.

After nine seasons as a member of the Baltimore Ravens with Harbaugh, Ricard followed the coach to the Giants in free agency.

Sunday, Ricard played 37 offensive snaps as the Giants ran 37 times for 165 yards (4.5 yards per attempt) and held the ball for 36:40.

If you haven’t done the math, 37 snaps per game for 17 games would come out to 629 snaps. Ricard played a career-high 698 snaps for the Ravens in 2022, the only time he surpassed 600 snaps. He played only 274 snaps last season.

“The jobs and the roles that he’s being asked to play are built into our offense,” Harbaugh said. “Not everybody has those, but a lot of people do.

“There’s a lot of things that Pat can do that nobody else can do. Nobody in the world can do some of the things that Pat Ricard can do. And that’s good for us. That’s unique for us. So, it helps us be who we are. It builds into our team persona, our team identity. And we love that. We love that about him as a player.”

Ricard’s job boils down to hitting guys on the other team. Hard. Clearing holes for running backs or keeping pass rushers off quarterback Jaxson Dart. He is forever trying to remind defenders why he has the nickname “Pancake Pat.”

“Whatever the coaches ask for me to do to help his team win, I’m going to do,” Ricard said. “I mean, look, I was an undrafted defensive lineman. I played D-line, I played offense, I played both sides of the ball. I played special teams. Line me up in the backfield, on the line, in the slot, have me do this, that. Whatever it is, I’m going to try my best.”

One thing Ricard’s job rarely includes is touching the ball. In 133 career regular-season games, Ricard has 11 carries and 49 pass receptions.

He doesn’t care. He knows what he is good at.

“I played defense for most of my life, so for me to play on offense, I (couldn’t) care less if I ever get the ball,” Ricard said. “For me, it’s all about, I want to impose my will on defenses, and I have the most fun when I’m pancaking people and I’m springing big blocks for my guys to have success, getting lots of points, getting a lot of first downs, winning.”

“If the ball comes my way, cool. If not, then I’m not going to be getting in (Matt) Nagy’s face like, ‘I need the ball,’ or getting mad at Jaxson for not giving me the ball. It’s fine by me because these guys that are on my team, they’re playmakers, dynamic, and I feel like they would be better with the ball in their hands and me blocking for them. So, that’s what I’m cool with.”

‘Secret sauce’

Ricard played both ways for the Ravens in his first three NFL seasons, totalling 225 snaps as a defensive tackle. He has been a full-time fullback since 2020.

“Early on, I didn’t play offense in college, so for me it was like they had to almost limit what I could do my first maybe couple years just because I was still learning the position and learning offense in general,” Ricard said. “But I feel like now it’s like I’ve been in – I’ve had (senior offensive assistant) Greg Roman as my run game coordinator, offense coordinator, and now being back in his scheme, it’s like there’s so much to build off of to where they can plug and piece me in any spots.”

Ricard really has one job. Block people, and do it with authority. At this point in his career, he can do it from just about every spot or angle imaginable. Sunday, he was in a true fullback alignment 15 times, was an inline tight end seven times, in the slot 11 times and aligned as a wide receiver four times.

“Motion me, shift me, to where – I’ve done it all to the point where I can execute it at a really high level to where I feel like that’s like what G-Ro (Greg Roman) said about me is like I’m like the spaghetti sauce on the offense,” Ricard said. “I’m like the secret sauce to where you put me in different spots to get the advantage, and I’m usually a mismatch of who I’m blocking because I’m usually bigger than them, to where I think it’s really an advantage for the offense.

“And it’s a lot of fun. It’s a lot of fun to be in this offense, to be moved around a lot in motion and shift and be in different spots. It’s almost like Where’s Waldo on Sundays, and it can be a lot for a defense to defend.”

The Giants’ way

The smashmouth style that Harbaugh has brought back to the Giants is reminiscent of the Giants’ championship teams of the Super Bowl era. Those teams generally dominated the line of scrimmage. They were gritty, not pretty. They had physical defenses. They had physical run games. And, by the way, they featured fullbacks.

The Bill Parcells teams had Maurice Carthon. The Tom Coughlin teams had Madison Hedgecock and Henry Hynoski.

When I posted the ‘Kudos and Wet Willies’ after Sunday’s victory over the Dallas Cowboys, I did not included Ricard in the ‘Kudos’. BBV commenters let me know about the oversight. Ricard has been feeling the love from Giants fans.

“I definitely felt it when I signed here and I’ve been around,” Ricard said. “But after this game, my social media has been flooding with just so much support from Giants fans just telling me how much they love how I play, MVP of the game, all this stuff. And I think it’s more of just how excited they are to have a fullback and the way I play.

“I’m all for it, I love it. I’m (going to) continue to play hard and do whatever I can to help the Giants keep getting wins.”

‘Hungry and humble’

New head coaches always bring a handful of their favorite players from prior coaching stops to help ease the transition and build a culture. Ricard is, of course, one of several ex-Ravens now wearing a Giants uniform.

Ricard has been impressed by his new teammates from the start.

“I just see how hungry and how humble everybody is here,” Ricard said. “They just – they want – there’s so many guys here that want to prove themselves. They want to win, and you just see it with how they work, how they prepare, and how much they love each other.

“I remember when I first got here for OTAs, just seeing how much the guys are cheering each other on in our running workouts and being there for one another and hanging out in the locker room two hours after we were done for the day. And I’m thinking, I’m like, ‘Wow, New York City is right across the river, right there, and guys would rather be in the locker room hanging out two hours after.’ So, I feel like that was just things I noticed right away, and I think it’s so important for a team to want to win and want to be crazed, loving one another and working hard.”

Hungry and humble is actually a great way to describe Ricard. Hungry to deliver pain to opposing defenses and win football games, and humble about how good he has been at his job for a decade now.

item.title: Lions Week 2 preview: Breaking down Bills’ offensive, defensive schemes
item.description: Breaking down the offensive and defensive schemes of the Buffalo Bills, the Detroit Lions’ Week 2 opponent.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills will square off in a “Thursday Night Football” battle to kick off Week 2. The Bills went through a coaching change this offseason, and while an internal promotion of Joe Brady to head coach kept their offense intact, hiring Jim Leonhard as defensive coordinator has the Bills’ defense shifting from a 4-2 to a 3-4 front.

Let’s take a closer look at the Bills’ coaching staff, the scheme they run, and some scouting notes from last week’s game along with some previously viewed games in 2025.

Bills head coach: Joe Brady

NFL coaching seasons: Entering ninth season in the NFL
Offensive coordinator: Four; Bills 2024-25 and Panthers 2020-21
Passing game coordinator: LSU 2019 (National Championship – QB Joe Burrow)
Influences: Sean Payton
Coached under: Payton (Saints), McDermott (Bills), Matt Rhule (Panthers), Ed Orgeron (LSU)
Playcaller: Yes

Dan Campbell coached alongside Brady during the 2017-18 seasons in New Orleans, and has this to say about the start to Brady’s head coaching career:

“I know Joe Brady very well. That’s a heck of a start there.”

Offensive coordinator: Pete Carmichael

NFL coaching seasons: Entering 27th season in the NFL
Offensive coordinator seasons: Entering 16th season
Previous coaching positions: Senior offensive assistant, passing game coordinator, QB coach, WR coach, TE coach
Influences: Sean Payton (20 seasons), Marty Schottenheimer, Pete Carmichael Sr. (Father)
Coached under: Payton (Saints, Broncos), Schottenheimer (Chargers, Washington), Chris Palmer (Browns)
Detroit staff connection: John Fox, Senior Assistant (with Lions in 2023)

Offensive scheme

Passing game: Pro-Spread
Running scheme: Man, Inside-Zone
Scouting notes:

  • Efficient offense due to success in the run game and quick pass completions
  • Spread philosophies at their core
  • Heavy influences from Payton (Saints) and Bengals-style (how they use Joe Burrow)
  • Week 1: 11 personnel 33% of snaps, 12 for 12%, 13 for 40%
  • Note: Bills spent so much time in 13 in Week 1 because Texans stayed in nickel sets
  • 60/40 pass-run split in Week 1
  • QB Josh Allen can throw to all levels of the field
  • Tested Texans deep in Week 1 more than he’s done in the past
  • Under center 65% of the time in Week 1
  • Play-action 41% of dropbacks in Week 1
  • Allen has 81 career rushing TDs (most among QBs in NFL history)
  • North-South rushing attack runs right at the teeth of the defense
  • Week 1 blocking percentages: Man roughly 40%, Inside-Zone 30%

Dan Campbell on Bills’ offense:

“Can’t say enough about this quarterback. He’s a catalyst for them. And it’s a good O-line. They’ve got weapons, and a good back.”

“They have three tight ends. They have three real guys that have three different roles that they’re all three pretty good at. And (Jackson Hawes) 85 can block a little bit. We liked him coming out and he proved to be a pretty good blocker last year. So, he’s kind of their heavy-Y. And then Dalton (Kincaid), 86, he’s a mismatch in the pass game, man. He’s one of these big skill, get through the defense, one-on-one matchups. And then (Dawson) Knox does it all. He does everything. He’s the guy, he’s the jack of all trades and he makes it right. He’s kind of the glue that, ‘What do you need? I’m the release guy, I’m the blocker, I’m the hybrid H-back, I’m the split me out one-on-one.’ He does it all.”

Defensive coordinator: Jim Leonhard

NFL seasons as a player: 10 years at safety (Bills, Ravens, Jets, Broncos, Saints, Browns)
NFL coaching seasons: 3 years in the NFL (8 in college)
Defensive coordinator seasons: First-year
Previous roles: DBs coach, passing game coordinator, assistant head coach (Broncos)
Influences: Rex Ryan, Mike Pettine, and Vance Joseph for scheme; Sean Payton for coaching style
Coached under: Payton (Broncos), Joseph (Broncos), Bret Bielema (Illinois), Paul Chryst (Wisconsin)
Played for: Pettine (Browns, Bills, Jets), Ryan (Jets, Ravens), Payton (Saints), John Fox (Broncos), Jack Del Rio (Broncos), John Harbaugh (Ravens), Dick Jauron (Bills)

Defensive scheme

Base: 3-4 Base, attacking front
Coverage: Zone-heavy
Scouting notes (from Week 1):

  • Defense modeled after the Broncos 3-4 attacking scheme
  • Big defensive shift after previously playing in a 4-2 front; required new personnel
  • Defensive philosophy switch will take time to adapt
  • 5-man front in base (3 down DL, 2 pass-rushing LB) – roughly 40% of defensive snaps in Week 1
  • 4-man front in subpackages (2 DL and 2 PR-LB) – roughly 60%
  • Vs. 11 personnel: faced 42 snaps, 25 in nickel (36% of snaps) and 17 in dime (24%)
  • Vs. 12, 13, and Jumbo: 30 snaps, 28 in Base defense (39%)
  • Picks and Stunts are foundations of pass rush
  • Pressure on 36% of passing snaps
  • Blitz 26% of snaps
  • Zone coverage around 80% — Cover-3 was highest at 31%, then Cover-6 (22%), Cover-4 (19%), Cover-2 (7%)
  • Man 18% —mainly Cover-2 (10%) and Cover-1 (8%)

Dan Campbell on Saints’ defense:

“This defensive line is their catalyst over there. (DT) Ed Oliver and (EDGE Greg) Rousseau, man, really good player. Length, explosive. They’ve got (EDGE Bradley) Chubb on the other end. Big boy in the middle, man. That’s an active defense and it was a big win for them (in Week 1).”

item.title: 6 NFL teams under the most pressure in Week 2
item.description: Many teams, player must rebound from a rough Week 1
item.content:encoded:
We’re onto Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season after a wild start of the season. As usual, Week 1 was unpredictable and there were plenty of surprises

Now, several teams (and players) need to regroup to avoid starting the season at 0-2 where the odds of making the decrease quite drastically. Here are the teams facing the most pressure in Week 2, presented in alphabetical order:

Dallas Cowboys

The Cowboys, seemingly like every year, were tabbed as a sexy Super Bowl contender in the offseason. They looked far from it in a 28-20 loss at the New York Giants on Sunday. The Giants, one of the worst teams in the league last season, were clearly the better team on Sunday night and outclassed Dallas. The Cowboys must bounce at home against the beatable Washington Commanders on Sunday to stay in the early mix in the NFC East.

Denver Broncos

The Broncos looked like a team that was in its first week of training camp going up against a team coming off a bye week in a 31-10 loss at the Kansas City Chiefs. The Broncos were out of sorts on both sides of the ball and did not look like one of the NFL’s best rosters, which was expected. This may just be a Week 1 thing. But the issue for the Broncos is their schedule. Their next four games are against the Jaguars, Rams, 49ers, Chargers and Seahawks. Denver better get it together at home against Jacksonville on Sunday.

Green Bay Packers

The Packers are in feeling the sting this week. They completely melted down in the fourth quarter against the Minnesota Vikings and Carson Wentz, of all people, on Sunday. The host Vikings scored 22 unanswered points in the fourth quarter to shock the Packers 39-22. To make matters worse, Green Bay was the only losing team in the stout NFC North in Week 1. If Green Bay stumbles at the very beatable New York Jets on Sunday, they will be digging themselves a big hole in the tough NFC.

Houston Texans

The Texans entered the season with the reputation of having one of, if not the very best, defenses in the NFL. Then, Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills hung 36 points on them. It was a classic games against two likely AFC heavyweights. The Texans’ offense looked strong in the 36-31 loss and the defense should be fine. But they have to show it Sunday at home against Joe Burrow and the Cincinnati Bengals. Losing two home games to start the season would be a blow to a team with Super Bowl hopes.

Los Angeles Rams

The Rams’ Super Bowl parade may be on hold. The darlings of the league were punched in the mouth by NFC West rival the San Francisco 49ers in Australia. The Rams were very sluggish in their whirlwind trip and then they lost new superstar toy Myles Garrett to a stint on the injured reserve. The Rams don’t have much time to fret, though. They host the upstart Giants on Monday night. This will not be an easy test for the Rams. But they most likely get their stuff together (they were out of sorts on both offense and defense against the 49ers) or they could be in a big hole in the NFC West, where the other three teams are all 1-0.

New England Patriots

The pressure here starts with quarterback Drake Maye. He followed up a tough Super Bowl appearance against Seattle to a rough performance against the Seahawks in Week 1. Frankly, Maye cost his team the game, ending it would baffling interception. Maye has to break out of his slump against a tough Pittsburgh Steelers’ defense on Sunday.

item.title: Stat was a bad way to start the season
item.description: The Denver Broncos lost the game in two of three phases on Monday – offensively and defensively. I would say that special teams was the only phase that the Broncos won. Jeremy Crawshaw forced the Kansas City Chiefs to start three drives inside their 10 (9, 6 and 3 yard lines). The Broncos only started […]
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos lost the game in two of three phases on Monday – offensively and defensively. I would say that special teams was the only phase that the Broncos won. Jeremy Crawshaw forced the Kansas City Chiefs to start three drives inside their 10 (9, 6 and 3 yard lines). The Broncos only started one drive inside the ten (on the 8). Marvin Mims averaged 18 yards on his two punt returns. That was about the end of the good for the Broncos.

The offense finished the game 2 of 12 on 3rd downs and 0 for 1 on 4th downs. The offense got only 9 first downs in the game and fumbled three times (only losing one). As crazy it seems, the Broncos are not the worst in the NFL after week 1 in terms of 3rd down conversion. The Browns are worst going 1 of 8 on first team in their game. When only the Browns are worse, you know it’s bad.

On the other side, the Chiefs had 19 first downs, and were 9 of 17 on third down. Defensively the Broncos are only seventh worst in 3rd down conversion rate allowed. The Cowboys allowed the Giants to convert on 9 of 11 which is crazy.

The Broncos had 58 actual defensive plays (KC had 3 kneel-downs) and somehow managed to miss a tackle on 29.8% of those plays. There were 34 solo tackles for the Broncos and 40 assisted tackles. Since missed tackle percentage does not delineate what play the missed tackle happened on (two can and did happen on multiple plays on Monday) we don’t know how many of those plays involved a missed tackle, but the Broncos had 24 missed tackles last night. Their were at least two on the TD pass to Rashee Rice.

According pro-football-reference.com the Broncos only had 85 missed tackles in the regular season in 2025.

The defense did end up getting two sacks (both by Zach Allen) who also had three QBhits to go with those sacks, meaning that he had at least five pressures in the game. The rest of the defense combined for two QBhits, one by Que Robinson and one by Jonah Elliss. Nik Bonitto did not show up in either stat, though he might have had a pressure. Admittedly he should have had plenty of them given that he was going up a player in Kahlil Benson who had never played a snap at LT above the high school level. Admittedly, the Chiefs were getting rid of the ball quickly on Monday, but he still should have had something to show. It’s possible that he had a pressure since those have not been tabulated yet.

According to NFL Next Gen stats, the Chief runners last night we getting -0.1 yards before contact, meaning that they were getting hit at or behind the LOS on most plays. They still managed to gain 223 yards on 35 actual runs on Monday (taking out the kneel-downs). That’s 6.37 yards per carry. That’s the second worst run defense in the league right now. Only the Panthers defense, which allowed 291 yards on 39 carries (7.46 ypc), was worse in week one.

item.title: Midweek Musings: Buckle Up, Bears Fans
item.description: Check out @gridironborn’s midweek musings, from Caleb Williams and Ben Johnson to PFF and the return of football.
item.content:encoded:
Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again:

The summer of 2026 was mostly a hot and humid mess in the Midwest. It rained a lot, the temps got uncomfortable early, and we were offered few reprieves. Then football started, and cooler weather arrived. We’re close to hoodie season. You can almost taste the apple cider. I love autumn, mainly for the football, but give me all the other good stuff that comes with it too.

I’ve never correctly advocated for a Chicago Bears head coach candidate before Chicago landed Ben Johnson – and I was extremely early. It was early in the 2023 season I started pushing it and when I dropped the idea on a Lions podcast, the hosts about kicked me off the show. I knew I had something at that moment. It’s given me an added layer of enjoyment to this new era of Bears football. I was extremely confident the Bears would be getting an offensive mastermind. I had no idea he’d be such a badass.

The new Nike Bears logo is incredible. I love this thing so freaking much. I might need to get another writing gig to help pay off all the gear I’m going to buy. Don’t tell my wife.

I was wrong about D’Andre Swift. I said he was a supercharged RB2 or a decent lead in a committee but he wasn’t a guy who could dominate in the run game. While that was the book on Swift before he landed in Chicago – and a fair representation of his work in 2024 – he’s been a much improved back under the Ben Johnson regime. It’s not often you see this type of growth this deep into a player’s career. Kudos to him for making it work.

I liked the Panthers jerseys – the black and Carolina Blue (or whatever they’re calling it) is a fun look. I just can’t understand choosing to wear dark colors on a hot day in September while letting your opponent where the traditional away whites. The temps were brutal. I wonder if they regret their uniform choice.

Speaking of the hot Carolina temps – did you catch Caleb Williams wiping his hand off mid-play to get a better grip on the football? I don’t think I’ve ever seen that before.

PFF put out a grade on Caleb Williams that sure looked like they didn’t watch the same game the rest of the world saw on Sunday. Really good reminder that the grades are an invention for engagement, as explained by their founder years ago. Engage in those grades at your own risk, positive or negative.

I said on Bear & Balanced this week that I thought that might’ve been one of Caleb’s best games as a pro. He looked completely in charge and had a steady, high-level performance. There are a couple of throws and runs that will make his end of season highlight reel, yes, but there were so many smart decisions on when to run, when to throw away, and when to check the ball down that were a work in progress last season. This is big trouble for the rest of the league and for those Caleb haters in your group chats.

If you’re just coming back to the site and missed my story on the history of the Chicago Bears mascots, I promise you it’s worth your time. These niche history dives are fun but always take more time than I think they will.

I thought the TD pass to Jahdae Walker was beautiful. The pass itself was a nice little schematic win, but the fact that Ben Johnson schemed up Walker after he did all the dirty work all game was one of those football moments where you know that guys are buying in and Johnson understands how to reward hard work. Football euphoria.

Did you notice that Carolina wanted nothing to do with Zavion Thomas on their kickoffs? I’m curious if that’s a trend we’ll see and, if so, whether there’s a way to call a better return play knowing they’ll be targeting the non-Zavion returner.

Plenty of hand-wringing over the defense, and I get it; we’ve come to expect a certain standard of living on the defensive side of the ball over the years. Let’s see where it goes over the next few weeks, but I want those of you who can’t help but lead with the negative to do me a favor and look up at the scoreboard once in a while. This is fun if you’re willing to join the rest of us.

I’m eager to get to the Vikings game. I have a lot of Vikings fans in my general orbit, and while we can all be happy for them reveling in their big win against Green Bay last week, it’s time to start making a statement with a divisional victory. I don’t really care who is playing quarterback; jump on this team early and dare them to play in the track meet with you. Pushing teams to get out of their comfort zone puts the ball in harm’s way and will allow the Bears to continue their dominance in the turnover differential.

Only 548 more points to break the 2013 Broncos mark…

item.title: AP Chiefs Mailbag: How concerning was the passing game against Denver?
item.description: Arrowhead Pride staff writer Jared Sapp answers your questions about Kansas City after a big win in Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag!Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs!

Coming off a monster 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football,” let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds.

TheSovereign1587 asks:

What specifically stood out the most about the passing game that made it look as rough as it did? Was it Patrick Mahomes being rusty? Did his knee affect his throwing ability/accuracy? Was it the WRs, not getting open, mistakes, etc? Were the pass plays and routes not effective?

Tackle play will take the bulk of the blame for the Chiefs’ disappointing results through the air Monday. That certainly played a role as rookie Kahlil Benson’s inexperience at left tackle significantly dictated the game plan. The uncertainty on the left side masked legitimate concerns about Jaylon Moore’s ability to man the right tackle spot.

However, I think other factors combined with Benson and Moore to make for a perfect storm against the Chiefs’ passing attack.

Mahomes definitely appeared rusty, especially in the first half. He looked like a player who had not been on the field competitively since December. In addition, wide receivers Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy played as they had been in and out of the lineup throughout training camp. Week 1 was essentially the preseason for the full starting offense.

Also, the Denver secondary — arguably the league’s best and a group very familiar with the Chiefs — deserves credit. The Broncos’ defensive backs apparently were Denver’s only unit that was aware a game was scheduled for Monday night.

I think Mahomes will get at least some of his timing back, the tackle play will improve, and most defensive backfields do not have the talent to match Denver’s game plan. However, I am taking real concerns from Monday night and am unsure how much it can be improved. I will probably wait until after Kansas City’s Week 5 bye to determine how panicked or confident to be.

RoyalsFanBill asks:

Will the Chiefs continue to feature the running game? Hope this isn’t the ole Marty Schottenheimer trick of starting a game with a deep pass only to not pass the rest of the game. I don’t think we will revert back to the old offense, but it would be my major question going forward.

Kenneth Walker is effectively signed to a two-year contract worth $28.7 million with a team option for a third year in 2028. I think the Chiefs plan to make him their workhorse over that period. Outside of Mahomes and defensive tackle Chris Jones, Kansas City’s biggest investment has been on the interior of their line.

With the money owed to Walker, center Creed Humphrey and guard Trey Smith, it would be incompetence not to rely on the run game early and often.

I do think we will see a bit more balance in the coming weeks. It also won’t surprise me if rookie Emmett Johnson sees more work in the backfield on a short week after Walker’s heavy Monday night workload. But I think the days of the run game being an afterthought in the Andy Reid offense are officially over.

ReadyForFBSeason asks:


What will other teams see on film that they can exploit? Denver clearly didn’t adjust well during the game. What will the Indianapolis Colts be preparing to do differently in Week 2?

The Broncos’ inability to answer Walker may be all that is keeping the Indianapolis Colts’ struggles against Derrick Henry of the Baltimore Ravens from becoming a major Week 1 story. Indianapolis gave up 324 passing yards and 202 yards on the ground. We will see what adjustments they make, but Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo — a longtime Mahomes nemesis — has a lot to fix in a week’s time.

One mistake on Denver’s part was abandoning the run game early and only having 11 rushing attempts by running backs. Expect the Colts to try to work around Kansas City’s rejuvenated pass rush with a heavy dose of tailback Jonathan Taylor — who totaled 121 scrimmage yards and a pair of touchdowns on Sunday.

wbenk307 asks:


Can we continue to expect that level of domination from our D-line and third down defense? Denver had the best offensive line last season, so I am wondering if this was Week 1 wonkiness or the tone for the rest of the year.

Broncos quarterback Bo Nix might still be having nightmares about Kansas City’s newfound pass rush when the teams meet again in Denver during Week 8. I think what the Chiefs did early on should be taken very seriously.

The most encouraging sign of the Chiefs’ defensive dominance came via the snap counts. Chris Jones, Peter Woods, R Mason Thomas, and Felix Anudike-Uzomah all made their presence felt while playing less than 60% of the defensive snaps. The timeshare approach may not lend itself to individual players putting up huge sack numbers, but the Broncos’ offensive line quickly proved more tired than the Chiefs’ defensive front, with fresh players constantly switched in.

George Karlaftis will assuredly lead the group in defensive snaps most weeks, but I expect his 86% snap count to trend down, likely inversely to Ashton Gillotte’s 27% trending up as his foot heals. The Chiefs have the players in place to imitate the constant rotation that helped the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots advance to last year’s Super Bowl.

Health will ultimately determine Kansas City’s defensive dominance. The Chiefs’ secondary worked around the absence of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane after the first defensive series. However, an effective pass rush needs top-notch defensive backs to be maximized.

The Chiefs’ defensive line played inspired against Denver, but it remains a group with little depth. With the current roster, even one injury could prove catastrophic to what the Chiefs want to do. Second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott will hopefully return from the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list soon after the bye. We will see if rookie edge rusher Jack Pyburn — recently claimed off waivers — can carve out a role this season. But Monday night’s group missing any round of rotational snaps could leave the defensive line very tired, very fast.

Papajazz asks


What are reasonable expectations going forward?

Week 1 is generally a terrible sample to use for the sweeping predictions people inevitably fire off immediately after. I am not going to predict the Chiefs to win the Super Bowl based on one game. I remain high on the Chiefs as a playoff team that should challenge for the AFC West title. The next few weeks should dictate our expectations.

In the short term, Kansas City came out on top of their seemingly toughest early-season matchup. It would be very disappointing if they enter the bye week (with the Colts, the Miami Dolphins, and the Las Vegas Raiders on tap) at anything less than 4-0.

Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! We will be back after the Chiefs’ season continues with the Colts on “Sunday Night Football.” Keep watchingThe Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.

item.title: 5 Lions to watch vs. Bills on TNF
item.description: Can Buffalo’s defense slow down a high-powered Detroit offense?
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills are set to take on the Detroit Lions on Thursday night, and they’ll look to open play at the new Highmark Stadium with a win. After slaying their demons down south by beating the Houston Texans in Houston for the first time since 2006, Buffalo is riding high to open the 2026 NFL season.

The Lions also won their first game, though they took a slightly different route to do so. Detroit needed overtime to dispatch the New Orleans Saints, holding on to win 31-30 in a back-and-forth contest. Neither the Bills nor the Lions were able to pull away from their respective opponents, and it’s likely that we’re set for an entertaining game between two of the more exciting offensive clubs in the league this season.

If the Bills are going to start this season 2-0, they’ll need to slow some of Detroit’s top players, and they have plenty of weapons to highlight. Here are five Lions to watch against the Bills this week.
_____________________________________________________________________________

RB Jahmyr Gibbs

Detroit’s top running back might wear number zero, but he’s arguably the best running back in the NFL right now. Equally dangerous as a runner and a receiver, Gibbs can hurt teams in a variety of ways. against New Orleans on Sunday, he totaled 156 rushing yards on a league-leading 29 carries. Nearly half of his rushing attempts resulted in a first down, as he achieved that mark a league-leading 14 times in Week One. As if averaging 5.4 yards per rush wasn’t impressive enough, Gibbs also totaled five receptions for 30 yards on five targets. That was actually a lower-end day for him as a receiver, as he has caught 186 passes for 1,479 yards and ten scores over the course of his career.

Now in his fourth year, Gibbs is the bellcow back for the first time, as his former running mate David Montgomery is now playing for Buffalo’s Week One opponent in Houston. Montgomery scored three times in the opener against the Bills, and while Buffalo limited his efficiency by holding him to three yards per carry, he doesn’t have nearly the same burst that Gibbs does. Buffalo needs to be disciplined in its run fits, and the defense needs to be much better overall when it comes to tackling. Otherwise, Gibbs will make them pay.

WR Amon-Ra St. Brown

The Saints kept St. Brown relatively quiet last week, and he still caught ten passes for 67 yards and two touchdowns on 14 targets in the game. He currently leads the league in targets, receptions, and receiving touchdowns. After Buffalo allowed Nico Collins to catch seven passes for 75 yards and a score last week on ten targets, they’ll face yet another challenge this week in trying to contain St. Brown. He can operate from multiple places on the field, and whether he’s inside or outside, he’s extremely dangerous.

Will defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard have top corner Christian Benford travel with him like Benford did with Collins on Sunday? Or, will Leonhard try a different strategy this week? With speedster Jameson Williams on the other side, it’s difficult to commit too many resources to one offensive target, and that’s without even discussing tight end Sam LaPorta. The Benford vs. St. Brown matchup is going to be tremendous on Thursday night.

G Ben Bartch

After starter Christian Mahogany suffered an injury, which looks likely to keep him out of action this week, Bartch filled in admirably against the Saints. However, with a backup center in Juice Scruggs already starting, the difficulty for Detroit’s offensive line is cranked up a notch this week. Second-year man Deone Walker was a tremendous problem for Houston on Sunday, as was veteran Ed Oliver.

Not only is the talent of Buffalo’s interior defensive line something to contend with, but the crowd noise is certainly to be amped up this week. Buffalo’s home crowd is always lively, but with Thursday night being the home opener in a brand-new stadium, I expect the twelfth man to make communication difficult for Detroit. Starting a few backup offensive linemen on the road isn’t ideal, and if Buffalo’s top-line unit can take advantage of some backups up front for the Lions, they can have a huge impact on the game.

DE Aiden Hutchinson

This guy is a monster. Just four days after having to deal with the combination of Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter, Buffalo will have to find a way to deal with Hutchinson, a former No. 2 overall pick. On Sunday against New Orleans, Hutchinson had two sacks, four quarterback hits, and two tackles for loss. That’s how you impact the game up front. Buffalo had a great protection scheme in that they used double-teams, slides, and chips to keep Houston’s edge rushers off balance.

They varied who was staying in to chip, and they kept switching who they double teamed, as well. The Bills will have to be just as disciplined in their plan to limit Hutchinson, as he is the kind of player who can single-handedly ruin a game plan. Left tackle Dion Dawkins and right tackle spencer Brown have to bring their A-game.

CB Rock Ya-Sin

A banged-up Detroit secondary is an area that Buffalo’s explosive passing offense should look to exploit this week. They’re already missing starting safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who are on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. Reserve safeties Thomas Harper and Christian Izien are also dealing with injuries, so players like Avonte Maddox and Chuck Clark have stepped into larger roles. That kind of unrest at the safety level puts stress on the corners, and Saints quarterback Tyler Shough picked on Ya-Sin last week.

On ten targets, Ya-Sin allowed seven catches for 52 yards and a touchdown for a passer rating against of 115.2. Buffalo looked like a completely different team passing the football last week thanks in large part to the addition of DJ Moore on the outside. He opens things up for everyone, as does tight end Dalton Kincaid. If Ya-Sin is one-on-one against anyone on Thursday, I assume that quarterback Josh Allen will take his shots.

item.title: The Chiefs dismantling the Broncos has some Colts fans sweating
item.description: The Colts have every right to be nervous about their game against the Chiefs.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos had one of the best defenses in 2025. It’s what carried them to a No. 1 seed in the AFC. Sure, it might have been a bit of a down year for the conference but there was no denying their defensive prowess. Teams change and personnel is different every year, but what the Kansas City Chiefs did to the Broncos on Monday Night Football should keep some Indianapolis Colts fans up at night. 

A ton of that concern comes from the Chiefs hanging 31 points on that defense. More concern comes from the fact that the Chiefs’ defense shut down Bo Nix and the Broncos’ offense as well. The most concerning part has nothing to do with either the Chiefs or the Broncos, however. The main concern stems from what we witnessed on Sunday against the Ravens as the Colts were absolutely shredded. 31 points were surrendered by halftime with Lamar Jackson having 324 yards through the air, while he and Derrick Henry picked up another 184 on the ground. Let’s also not forget that Zay Flowers had 150 yards and barely played half a game.

Overall, the defense couldn’t get off the field. Third and long was no problem as the Ravens converted with ease, especially in the first half. Justin Walley was targeted on repeat and left the game cooked. The line didn’t generate enough pressure and failed to tackle Jackson when they had the chance. Flowers, Henry, and even Mark Andrews ran free and wild. If the Chiefs took the Broncos to the woodshed, they must be licking their chops after witnessing that incredibly lackluster effort from the Colts. 

The season isn’t over by any stretch of the imagination, and no one in the organization should panic. One good game gets them right back into things. To be without nerves after watching each team play, however, would be foolish. One team looked primed for another go at a Super Bowl. The other looked like they will be watching the playoffs from home again. Something has to change if the Colts are going to win at Arrowhead.

item.title: Drake Maye ready to bounce back against the Steelers in Week 2
item.description: The Patriots starting quarterback is looking to rebound from a three-interception outing in Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
Drake Maye had a forgettable regular season opener, tossing three interceptions in his final three possessions to seal a 13-10 New England Patriots loss to the Seattle Seahawks. However, there is no time to dwell on those mistakes: Week 2 against the Pittsburgh Steelers awaits.

And for Maye, it will be an opportunity to bounce back against a team that qualified for the playoffs in 2025. So, how is he planning on doing that? By bringing the proper mindset to the preparation.

“We’re on to Pittsburgh. We have another week and another chance in this league. That’s dealing with the ups and downs in this league. That’s part of playing in the National Football League,” Maye said during an appearance on WEEI earlier this week.

“It’s just part of being an athlete at a professional level. My brothers and my dad played sports in college and have done things, and you have teammates — that’s what we have teammates for and coaches. They’ve experienced it. And at this capacity it’s just different when you’re playing this position at quarterback. Your mistakes and what you do with the football is at a more drastic level because your decisions change the outcomes of games. Just realizing that and also realizing that you got to go back out there and and have a next-play mentality.”

Maye started the Patriots’ season opener fairly well, executing the take-what-the-opponent-gives-you game plan and helping his team head into the fourth quarter up 10-3. However, things fell apart from that point on.

By his own admission, the third-year quarterback “lost patience” and ended up costing his game a possible victory and 1-0 start to the season. Against Pittsburgh, a similar outcome would put the reigning AFC champions under quite a bit of pressure already at this early stage in the season.

Maye, however, is not letting that outlook impact his work leading up to Week 2.

“He’s a guy who has a lot of confidence,” said left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker, who himself had a challenging first game. “We pat him on the back. We got him. We’re always riding for him, but he’s the type of guy who doesn’t really need that. He’s able to fix things on his own and come ready to work the next week.”

“He’s been great,” added tight end Hunter Henry. “He sometimes takes too much of the burden. I think we all can be better. We all have to look at ourselves in the mirror. Obviously, we can’t turn the ball over, and he knows that. But, maybe if we finish a little longer, we run better routes, we block a little better, protect a little better, some of those things don’t come into play. We all have to be better. It’s not on just one guy. This is a complete team sport and that’s the beauty of football. Excited to go out there and compete with him again this weekend.”

item.title: Purdue Boilermakers in the NFL: Week 1
item.description: How did the NFL Boilers do in week 1?
item.content:encoded:
The first week of the NFL season has come and gone and thanks to my purchase of NFL Sunday Ticket (not a sponsored post but I’m willing to listen) I can watch every game I want to. For me that mostly means I’m going to be able to watch my beloved Tampa Bay Bucs (shout out Mike Alstott) but it also means that anytime a Boilermaker is putting on a show in the NFL I can flip over and check them out. So, like we’ve done in the past we are gonna give you a one stop shop for all things NFL Boilermakers right here.

Unfortunately, the number of Boilermakers on active NFL rosters is down to just five. Not a great number. Who are the five you ask?

  • Derrick Barnes – Detroit Lions
  • George Karlaftis – Kansas City Chiefs
  • Payne Durham – Tampa Bay Bucs
  • Tyrone Tracy Jr. – New York Football Giants
  • Marcus Mbow – New York Football Giants

Purdue also has a few players hanging around practice squads and the like as well. That list is:

  • Aidan O’Connell – Las Vegas Raiders
  • Reese Taylor – Miami Dolphins
