item.title: Bengals vs. Buccaneers: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly
item.description: There was a lot to like from the Bengals in their Week 1 win over the Buccaneers.
item.content:encoded:
The Bengals opened the 2026 season with a win, and for once, the defense had a lot to do with it.

There were some familiar warts along the way, but Cincinnati made enough plays to hold off Tampa Bay, 33-27, at Paycor Stadium.

Whew. A Week 1 game that actually ended with the Bengals on the happy side of things.

Here are the best and worst from Cincinnati’s season-opening win.

The Good

The defense came to play

Well, hello there.

After everything we heard about Cincinnati’s rebuilt defense during the offseason, we finally got to see it against an actual NFL offense. And the unit immediately made its presence felt.

The Bengals forced fumbles on three consecutive Tampa Bay possessions in the first half. Myles Murphy strip-sacked Baker Mayfield, and Demetrius Knight Jr. scooped it up and returned it 27 yards for a touchdown.

Then Bryan Cook forced a fumble from Bucky Irving, with Boye Mafe recovering. A few plays later, Joe Burrow found Mike Gesicki for a touchdown.

On the next Tampa possession, Barrett Carter forced another Mayfield fumble near the goal line, and Cook recovered it in the end zone.

Three straight possessions. Three turnovers.

Cincinnati eventually forced four fumbles and recovered all four, while also sacking Mayfield four times. The Bengals turned those takeaways into 24 points.

That’s a pretty good way to start a new defensive era. 

Mike Gesicki was exactly what Cincinnati needed

Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins weren’t exactly having their usual Sunday. So, naturally, Mike Gesicki decided to have a day.

Gesicki caught five passes for 78 yards and a touchdown on seven targets, leading Cincinnati in receiving. He also came up big late in the first half, catching three passes for 52 yards on the drive that ended with an Evan McPherson field goal.

The Bucs spent plenty of attention on Chase and Higgins, and Burrow simply went somewhere else with the football.

That’s what makes this offense so interesting. If defenses want to take away Cincinnati’s two star receivers, there are going to be opportunities for guys like Gesicki to make them pay. 

Chase Brown and the run game

This was not the old-school Bengals running the ball 40 times and winning 17-13. But it was a much more balanced attack.

Cincinnati ran the ball 27 times and threw it 35 times, and Chase Brown finished with 16 carries for 56 yards and a touchdown. He also caught five passes for 23 yards.

More importantly, the Bengals showed a willingness to use the run as something other than a change of pace.

Brown’s five-yard touchdown run capped an 80-yard, 12-play drive in the second quarter and pushed Cincinnati’s lead to 21-3.

If Dan Pitcher’s offense really is going to lean into a more balanced approach in 2026, Sunday was a pretty encouraging first look.

Money Mac is back

Evan McPherson had himself a day. Four field goals. Four makes.

Twenty yards. Thirty-two yards. Fifty-five yards. Fifty-eight yards.

Those last two are particularly important because Tampa Bay had started to make things uncomfortable. Cincinnati wasn’t consistently finishing drives with touchdowns, but McPherson kept adding points.

He accounted for 12 of the Bengals’ 33 points and gave Cincinnati some breathing room when the offense wasn’t quite clicking.

Oh, and the 58-yarder was just ridiculous. It’s nice having that in your back pocket again. 

The offensive line quietly did its job

This probably won’t generate nearly as many headlines as a scoop-and-score or a 58-yard field goal, but it might be one of the more important things to come out of this game.

Joe Burrow was sacked just once.

He finished 25-of-35 for 254 yards, one touchdown and one interception, while completing passes to nine different receivers.

There were still some issues, but Burrow generally had enough time to work through his reads. Considering how much of Cincinnati’s success ultimately depends on keeping No. 9 upright, that’s a pretty significant development.

Sometimes the best thing an offensive line can do is make you forget it’s there. Sunday was one of those days. 

The Bad

Joe Burrow’s pick-six

There’s no way around this one. Burrow had a pretty solid afternoon overall, but his third-quarter interception was brutal.

With Cincinnati leading 27-13, Burrow tried to hit Andrei Iosivas, and Tampa Bay linebacker Josiah Trotter stepped in front of the pass and took it 27 yards for a touchdown.

Just like that, a 14-point game became a seven-point game. It wasn’t the kind of mistake that cost Cincinnati the game, but it absolutely gave Tampa Bay life when the Bucs needed it.

Burrow finished with 254 yards and a touchdown, so this wasn’t some disaster of a performance. But that interception was a bad one, and he’ll know it.

The good news? The Bengals responded.

The defense still missed too many tackles

Four forced fumbles and four sacks will get you a lot of attention. But this wasn’t a flawless defensive performance.

Cincinnati missed tackles, and Tampa Bay was able to move the football despite the turnovers. The Bengals also committed multiple offsides penalties, which is the kind of self-inflicted stuff that can become a real problem against better teams.

That’s the tradeoff with an aggressive defense. You want guys flying around trying to make plays. You also need them to know where the line is.

Cincinnati found that line a few times Sunday—and stepped over it. 

Ja’Marr Chase was basically a decoy

Two catches. Twelve yards. Four targets.

That’s it for Ja’Marr Chase.

Obviously, this isn’t going to happen every week. Tampa Bay made a concerted effort to take Chase away, and Burrow responded by distributing the ball elsewhere.

That’s actually a positive development.

Still, there’s a difference between taking Chase away and simply not getting him involved. The Bengals didn’t need Chase to win this game. But there will be Sundays when they absolutely will.

The offense left some points out there

Cincinnati scored 33 points, so complaining about the offense feels a little ridiculous.

Still, there were stretches where the Bengals had opportunities to put Tampa Bay away and couldn’t quite do it.

The Bengals went 2-for-5 in the red zone, according to the game statistics. That’s an area that could come back to bite them against a team that doesn’t hand them four turnovers.

The offense did enough. But it didn’t exactly leave the Bucs’ defense picking up the pieces. 

The Ugly

That pick-six made this way too interesting

This is where things got uncomfortable.

Cincinnati was up 27-13. Tampa Bay had struggled to protect the football. The Bengals’ defense was flying around.

Then Burrow threw the pick-six. Suddenly it was 27-20.

The Buccaneers had momentum, the crowd had gotten a little quieter, and everybody watching was thinking the same thing:

Please don’t do this.

Fortunately, McPherson answered with a 58-yard field goal, and the defense eventually forced its fourth turnover of the afternoon.

But Cincinnati turned what could have been a comfortable fourth quarter into a game that required some actual late-game execution. 

Tampa Bay wouldn’t go away

Credit to the Bucs. After falling behind 24-10 at halftime, Tampa Bay kept hanging around. The Buccaneers cut the lead to seven in the third quarter, and Baker Mayfield eventually ran for an eight-yard touchdown with 3:19 left to make it 33-27.

That’s when Cincinnati finally got the kind of close-out drive it has been looking for. The Bengals possessed the ball for the final 3:19 and didn’t give Tampa Bay another opportunity.

So, yes, it got ugly. But Cincinnati actually finished the job.

And honestly, after some of the fourth-quarter endings Bengals fans have endured over the years, I’ll take an ugly close-out over another meltdown every single time. 

Outlook: Week 1 was fun—Now comes the hard part

The Bengals are 1-0.

The defense looked different. The offense showed some balance. McPherson looked like McPherson again. Burrow made some good throws, made one really bad one, and Cincinnati still walked away with a six-point victory.

That’s a pretty good starting point. But there’s plenty to clean up.

The missed tackles need to improve. The penalties need to stop. The red-zone offense needs to be better. And Burrow probably isn’t going to get away with throwing a pick-six every week.

Then again, that’s why you play the games. For one Sunday, at least, the Bengals looked like a team that could win in more than one way.

Now let’s see if they can do it again.

item.title: Cowboys news: Jerry Jones wants better communication on defense
item.description: Here is today’s Dallas Cowboys news
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys spent the entire offseason saying Christian Parker would elevate communication on defense. That was his bread and butter. Jerry and Stephen Jones echoed that it was a leading reason they hired him.

On Sunday night, the Cowboys owner was left disappointed by how bad it looked against the New York Giants. Dallas needs to correct the communication issues soon, or else the season could go sideways fast.

Here is the latest news around the Dallas Cowboys.

Jerry Jones ‘disappointed’ in Cowboys’ opener, communication struggles – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com

Jerry Jones sounded very frustrated looking back at how the Cowboys defense lost Week 1.

Jones was asked what bothered him more: The communication problems, or New York’s ability to win more up front?

“Communication,” Jones said. “The communication aspects of it. Just being out of position. Fundamentally between the two, communication…”

“I was taken back that the physicalness of it wasn’t more obvious. We had some guys play hard, and we had some guys do some good things on both sides of the ball, offense and defense. But I was really surprised and dismayed, as all fans were, that we couldn’t basically stop some of that outside stuff. I was frustrated that we didn’t get more out of our running game which would’ve helped us more in our passing game.”

Did Dallas Cowboys have unrealistic expectations for Christian Parker, defense? Brian Schottenheimer says no – Clarence Hill Jr., DLLS Cowboys

Despite a down week, Brian Schottenheimer remains optimistic about who Christian Parker can become this year.

“I have no question Christian Parker is the right guy for this job,” Schottenheimer said. “He’s an outstanding coach. He will learn from this, just like our young players are going to learn from this. We’re going to play our young players this weekend too, and they’re going to play better and Christian’s going to call a better game this week and feel better about it. So experiences gained by making mistakes and unfortunately we made too many mistakes last night. That’s why we came up on the short end of the stick.”

Cowboys defensive leaders fueled by sense of urgency in Week 2 – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com

The Cowboys leadership council has some heavy lifting to do this week.

“Do your job, and at the end of the day, communicate,” [Kenny] Clark added. “. … I don’t think it was a problem with the physicality. I think, up front, we really played the blocks well, and most of the guys, what we’ve been talking about, too, is finding ways to do more. We’ve got to just do more.”

item.title: Kyle Monangai helped the Bears make NFL history and earned his spot as a Week 1 Secret Superstar
item.description: Chicago's record 59-37 rout wasn't the only surprise: a 49ers trade addition finally gave San Francisco's pass rush life, and a Commanders special teamer delivered one of the most viral hits of the young season.
item.content:encoded:
Superstars may lead the discussion when it comes to success in the NFL, but more often than not, it’s the guys you barely know who will make the plays needed when they’re needed. Such players can be underrated for all kinds of reasons. Perhaps they’re playing in a smaller market, and the media isn’t appropriately trumpeting their exploits. Maybe they’re hidden in a depth chart behind bigger names who may not be doing as much. Or, it’s always possible that a wayward coach hasn’t quite figured out that one guy needs elevation to bring better results to the team.

Whatever the reason, we at SB Nation always like to bring the underrated names to you with the offseason Hidden Gems and in-season Secret Superstars series.

And with that in mind, here are our NFC Secret Superstars for Week 1 of the 2026 regular season. And if you haven’t yet, download the new SB Nation app, so you can better read and comment on our stuff wherever you are!

Kyle Monangai, RB, Chicago Bears

Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson has never received the credit he deserves for designing one of the best and most diverse run games in the NFL.

This was the case when David Montgomery and Jahmyr Gibbs were running wild with Johnson as the Detroit Lions’ offensive coordinator in 2022 through 2024, and it’s the case now. Everybody wants to talk about Caleb Williams’ explosive passing plays and overall development, and that’s understood, but Johnson is right up there with Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay and whoever else as a run game genius, and that was never more apparent than in Chicago’s 59-37 demolition of the Carolina Panthers’ defense in Week 1.

Not only did the Bears set a franchise record for the most points ever in a season opener — pretty impressive when your franchise has been around in one form or another since 1920 — but they also participated in the highest-scoring Week 1 game in pro football history. Yes, Williams was impressive through the air, completing 21 of 29 passes for 269 yards, two touchdowns, no interceptions, and a passer rating of 124.1.

All well and good, but it was the Bears’ run game that gave the Panthers fits, with 39 carries for 291 yards (7.5 yards per carry), and SIX rushing touchdowns. D’Andre Swift was the main man with 18 carries for 129 yards and three scores, but in terms of explosiveness, it was second-year man Kyle Monangai who really set the tone. He gained 100 yards on 10 carries, and averaged an amazing 8.4 yards after contact. Most of that came on his 61-yard touchdown run late in the third quarter, but you could see it all over the tape.

The ways in which tight end Cole Kmet, as well as receivers Jahdae Walker and Luther Burden III, blocked on the play told you everything you need to know about how much everybody in the building values that run game.

“I saw Jahdae chasing down and making sure that wasn’t just a big play, but a touchdown,” Raymond said postgame. “I mean, it’s a huge play for Kyle, but Jahdae’s out there taking guys to make sure it happens. I mean, it goes from a big play, a first down to a touchdown. That’s a testament to the guys blocking. I think Lu had a big block too … so just all the stuff working together, and that’s what you want, especially for the backs we have.”

And the schemes they have. Bears opponents already know what others are just waking up to realize — that Ben Johnson would be noteworthy if all he did was to design the ground game.


Osa Odighizuwa, DL, San Francisco 49ers

Last season, the 49ers’ pass rush splits with and without Nick Bosa, who missed the last 14 games of the 2025 regular season with a torn ACL were about what you’d expect.

Per Sumer Sports:

With Bosa on the field (65 opposing dropbacks faced):

  • 3 sacks (4.62% sack rate)
  • 26 pressures (40.0% pressure rate)

With Bosa off the field (569 opposing dropbacks faced):

  • 17 sacks (2.99% sack rate)
  • 172 pressures (30.23% pressure rate)

This wasn’t just a testament to Bosa’s greatness; it was also an unfortunate statement about the rest of that defensive line. Bryce Huff led the team with five sacks and 46 total pressures, and only Huff and fellow edge defender Sam Okuayinonu had more than 30 total pressures. San Francisco’s interior defensive line was especially problematic from a pass rush perspective — Jordan Elliott, Alfred Collins, CJ West, Kalia Davis, and Kevin Givens combined for four sacks and 55 pressures, and when the entire guts of your pass rush is that light, it’s a severe problem.

Which is why in March, the 49ers traded a 2026 draft pick for ex-Dallas Cowboys interior disruptor Osa Odighizuwa and the four-year, $80 million contract he signed in 2025. Odighizuwa is a relative bargain on a $5.122 million cap hit in 2026, but the obligations shoot up to $23.407 million in both 2027 and 2028 if he’s still on the roster.

Based on what the 6’2”, 280-pound Odighizuwa did in his 49ers debut as his new team clocked the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 in Melbourne, Australia, there shouldn’t be any worries about his ability to live up to the deal. Odighizuwa has generally been more of a guy who racks up pressures than sacks — he had three takedowns and 52 pressures last season for Dallas’ abysmal defense — and that played out against the Rams. While Odighizuwa didn’t have a sack, all five of his quarterback pressures resulted directly in Matthew Stafford incompletions.

If you had a cornerback who could guarantee an o-fer from the reigning NFL Most Valuable Player every time he was involved in a play, that would be pretty nice, no? In this case, it was Osa Odighizuwa’s ability to blow stuff up along multiple gaps that really stood out, as long as you were paying attention to more than just sack totals.

Tyler Owens, Special Teams, Washington Commanders

How often does a special teams play go viral?

Well, one did on Sunday.

With 8:57 left in the first half of the Washington Commanders’ eventual 24-22 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles, Washington punted to Philly on fourth-and-18 from its own 19-yard line. That gave Commanders safety Tyler Owens the opportunity to blast through a double team “vice” consisting of receiver Darius Cooper and cornerback Jonathan Jones, and absolutely blast return man Michael Carter II on a 12-yard return.

It was a heroic effort, and Commanders head coach Dan Quinn had quite a bit to say about it on Monday.

“I didn’t see the start of it on the field,” Quinn recalled. “Might have caught like the corner where he beat the vice to go down the field, but I did see the tackle. And he had actually made a play earlier on punt as well where he had a tackle in a similar spot where he had beat a vice and went all the way inside. So, that’s the mark of a good gunner when they’re trying to vice you.

“It was one of the proudest plays for me of him, though. He’s a guy who’s speed and strain is always there, but to see that one come together, it was just awesome. And it was so him, like, ‘Oh, thanks, man. That’s what I do. ’ You know, like it was like no big deal. And you’re like, ‘Man, this is a really big deal. ’ It was a really cool play, and I got to see it probably like everybody else did from the network feed afterwards. And it was one of my favorite plays in a long time on special teams for sure.”

Owens did indeed have a similar play earlier in the game. With 7:42 left in the first quarter, the Commanders punted on fourth-and-10 from their own six-yard line, and this time, Owens went around the vice to stop returner Britain Covey for a one-yard loss.

Everybody loved what the 2024 undrafted free agent defensive back from Texas Tech did.

Owens has just 67 regular-season defensive snaps in his NFL career, but if he keeps dominating on special teams like this, he will absolutely stick and stay as a crucial part of Washington’s roster.

item.title: Examining the roster ties between Patriots, Steelers ahead of Week 2
item.description: The ex-Patriots and ex-Steelers set for Sunday at Gillette Stadium.
item.content:encoded:
Some former New England Patriots and former Pittsburgh Steelers will meet again at Gillette Stadium.

Between the active rosters, practice squads and reserve lists, four players in the fold this September have been members of both clubs during their NFL careers.

With stays ranging from days to years, here’s a glance through those ties ahead of Sunday’s 1 p.m. ET home opener.

PITTSBURGH

Brandon Smith, wide receiver — The Patriots signed Smith to the practice squad last December. The 27-year-old wide receiver’s stay ended with his release ahead of the AFC divisional round in January. A futures contract with the Steelers arrived 48 hours later, and he was retained on Pittsburgh’s practice squad at its formation following the NFL’s 53-man roster deadline in August. Undrafted out of Iowa in 2021, Smith made previous stops with the Dallas Cowboys, DC Defenders, Arizona Cardinals and New York Jets. He has made three appearances as a standard elevation.

Bradyn Swinson, outside linebacker — As the NFL’s cutdown deadline closed in, the Patriots waived a member of the 2025 draft class. Swinson subsequently went through the wire unclaimed en route to joining the Steelers’ initial practice squad. Taken in the fifth round at No. 146 overall last year, the 24-year-old former transfer from Oregon to LSU began his rookie campaign on the practice squad. He earned a promotion to the 53-man roster in November and went on to appear in four matchups, including the AFC Championship Game, handling 27 snaps on defense, 31 snaps on special teams and one solo tackle.

Christian Kuntz, long snapper — Once a linebacker prospect by way of Duquesne, Kuntz entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2017 and became an August addition in Foxborough. He was waived following that year’s preseason finale as the roster reduced from 90. Kuntz proceeded to log stints with Denver Broncos, Jacksonville Jaguars and Dallas Renegades on the way to converting to long snapper. The 32-year-old has since had a hand in Pittsburgh’s operation for 86 games dating back to his 2021 debut. Kuntz has made 11 tackles on special teams during his AFC North tenure.

NEW ENGLAND

Robert Spillane, linebacker — Now a back-to-back Patriots captain, Spillane has appeared in 100 games, including 64 starts, since breaking into the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2018. Originally signed by the Tennessee Titans after serving as a rookie minicamp tryout, the Western Michigan product went on to spend four years in Pittsburgh while cutting his teeth on special teams and as a sub-package linebacker. He moved on to the Las Vegas Raiders in 2023 and Foxborough in 2025. Spillane’s run has spanned 602 tackles and 9.5 sacks, plus two forced fumbles, two fumble recoveries, eight interceptions and one touchdown return. A pick and a team-high 15 tackles were in the cards last September when the Steelers visited Gillette Stadium.

item.title: Matthew Stafford, Sean McVay need to fix the Rams' suddenly broken offense
item.description: One bad game doesn't mean the season is over, but for a Rams team set on a Super Bowl-or-bust trajectory, they can't afford another prime-time stumble.
item.content:encoded:
Don’t be distracted.

In the aftermath of the Rams’ humiliating season-opening defeat in Australia, the team’s defense is dominating the news cycle: edge rusher Myles Garrett’s knee surgery, lineman Aaron Donald’s potential season debut.

But as coach Sean McVay prepares his team for Monday night’s game against the New York Giants, the Super Bowl-favorite Rams’ suddenly not-so-super offense also demands scrutiny.

Consider: Every starter is back from a unit that in 2025 led the NFL in offense and scoring, including quarterback Matthew Stafford, the reigning NFL most valuable player.

And yet the Rams managed just 190 yards and scored one touchdown in their 27-7 loss to the San Francisco 49ers.

That’s it.

Read more:Sean McVay unsure when Myles Garrett will return or when Aaron Donald will play

It was the fewest points scored by the Rams since a 20-3 loss to the Green Bay Packers in November 2023.

The Rams’ decision to arrive in Melbourne the day before the game appeared to leave them in a stupor.

Granted, 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris knows McVay and the Rams well. Morris was the Rams’ defensive coordinator from 2021-2023, and he is one of McVay’s closest friends. In December, as the coach of the Atlanta Falcons, he schemed his team to a 27-24 victory over the Rams.

But that’s no excuse for the Rams’ dreadful performance on offense against the 49ers.

The Rams’ first play proved an omen: 49ers linebacker Fred Warner nearly intercepted Stafford’s pass.

Stafford, an 18th-year pro, never found his rhythm. He completed only 15 of 25 passes for 155 yards. The 49ers turned a second-quarter interception into a touchdown drive.

That doesn’t mean the ability of 38-year-old Stafford appears to be falling off a cliff.

It was one game. He was out of sync. A player who is rewriting the NFL record book is more likely to come back and torch the Giants than to have two poor performances in a row.

“Plenty of stuff to clean up,” Stafford said. “Things to look at. We’ll make sure we’ll be ready to roll.”

The offense works best when running backs Kyren Williams and Blake Corum are gaining yardage in chunks, and McVay is calling plays that create space for receivers Puka Nacua and Davante Adams to make routine and sometimes spectacular catches.

Corum rushed for a team-best 54 yards, Williams had 41 yards and a touchdown.

Neither got an opportunity when the Rams faced a critical fourth-and-goal situation at the one-yard line. Neither did Nacua, who nearly scored on a catch the play before. Or Adams, who led the NFL with 14 touchdown catches last season, 11 from 10 yards or closer, including four from the one-yard line.

Instead, McVay called for a quarterback sneak.

The 49ers stopped Stafford short of the goal line, and the 49ers subsequently drove 99 yards for a touchdown.

Nacua, the NFL receptions leader last season, and Adams combined for eight catches for 100 yards, far below their typical performances.

And don’t forget the tight ends.

McVay, apparently, did just that.

About midway through the 2025 season, the Rams began regularly deploying as many as three tight ends at a time — and using them as targets. Colby Parkinson became one of Stafford’s primary targets and scored eight touchdowns, quadrupling his previous career best.

The Rams began this season with second-year pro Terrance Ferguson poised for a breakout.

Read more:Bill Plaschke knows his Rams perfect prediction was the worst. Will he stop now?

Parkinson and Davis Allen each caught one pass, Ferguson none. Veteran Tyler Higbee caught two passes, but lost a fumble that all but sealed the victory for the 49ers.

With 11 days between games, McVay, his staff and the players are intent on avoiding a repeat performance.

“The big area of focus improvement will be in regard to the pass game and some of the different things that we can do collectively,” McVay said. “It always starts with me.”

The defeat by the 49ers was only the third time in 10 seasons that McVay lost a season opener. Only once under McVay have the Rams started with two losses: In 2024, after losing in overtime at Detroit, the Arizona Cardinals routed them 41-10.

That team rebounded from a 1-4 start to reach the NFC divisional round.

That won’t be good enough for this Rams team, which was built to win Super Bowl LXI at SoFi Stadium.

With an offense now in need of a restart.
